"Whatever anyone requires, let them come to my house."
Thereafter, they exhaust their households to practice renunciation.

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me:
"Son of a householder!
A great assembly of giving should not be conducted as you have arranged it.
You should instead hold an assembly for the gift of Dharma; what use is there for an assembly of material gifts?"
This is the second point regarding the purpose of the reproach.
As for why Vimalakīrti waited until the seventh day was complete before coming to offer his reproach, there are generally three meanings:

first, because the worldly gift had already been completed and he was about to advance with the gift of Dharma, he first criticized what had been provided in order to clarify that there is a deficiency in the two types of giving.

Second, the seven-day period has reached its full term; once it is complete, success is achieved, and upon achievement, there is inevitably attachment. Therefore, he came after seven days to rebuke him. Third, both Śrīgupta and Vimalakīrti act for the benefit of sentient beings:
Śrīgupta bestows material wealth, while Vimalakīrti bestows the Dharma. Had Śrīgupta not first enticed him with wealth, there would have been no one to guide him with the Dharma.
The reason for using the gift of Dharma to censure the gift of wealth is that the gift of wealth nourishes the physical body, whereas the gift of Dharma nourishes the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the gift of wealth yields retribution only within the desire realm, while the gift of Dharma yields retribution within the three realms as well as beyond the three realms.
Furthermore, material giving has a sequence of before and after, whereas the gift of Dharma has no such sequence.
Moreover, material giving is exhaustible, while the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, material giving can be performed by both the ignorant and the wise alike, whereas the gift of Dharma is understood only by those who possess wisdom.
Therefore, I rebuked him with the Dharma, saying:
"Householder! I say this to you:..."
"What is called the assembly of the Dharma-gift?
The assembly of the Dharma-gift is that which simultaneously makes offerings to all sentient beings without before or after; this is called the assembly of the Dharma-gift."
The gift of material wealth cannot be used universally at once.
There are two kinds of the gift of Dharma:
the first is preaching the Dharma for others, which is called the gift of Dharma.
This means that what is expounded by a single sound reaches everywhere at once.
Second, because every single practice undertaken by a bodhisattva is for the benefit of all sentient beings, there is no sequence of before or after.
Furthermore, just as when one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, the ten directions are simultaneously taken as the object;
because one bestows gifts equally at once, there is no sequence of before or after.
"What does this mean? [It means that]..."
That is to say, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) by means of bodhicitta.

Since the preceding section on the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) explains that the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is established through this mind of loving-kindness, it is explained first.
Furthermore, because the four immeasurable minds can simultaneously and universally take the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as their object, they are explained first.
Ordinary worldlings give rise to loving-kindness for the sake of being reborn in the Brahma Heaven;
those of the Two Vehicles do so to seek merit;
and Bodhisattvas do so to seek the Buddha-way and to liberate sentient beings.
Now, wishing to cause them to seek the Buddha-way so as to give rise to a mind of compassion, it is said that one gives rise to a mind of compassion by means of the characteristic of bodhi.
Furthermore, since compassion desires to bestow happiness, this involves bestowing upon sentient beings the happiness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, one gives rise to loving-kindness through bodhicitta; this is also true loving-kindness, for it can truly benefit sentient beings.
"One gives rise to the mind of great compassion in order to rescue sentient beings."
The compassionate mind aims at uprooting suffering; if one regards actual salvation as compassion, then that compassion is truly great.
"By upholding the True Dharma, one gives rise to a joyful mind."
One desires that both oneself and others uphold the True Dharma, and thus takes joy in its arising.
Furthermore, one rejoices fundamentally because one delights in their attainment of freedom from what is not the Dharma; this is a mind that dwells upon the Dharma.
If one takes joy in upholding the True Dharma, this is the reality of joy.
"By means of gathering wisdom, one practices the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle practice the mind of equanimity in order to abandon enmity toward both enemies and kin.
Now, I wish to cause them to attain equanimous wisdom, renouncing everything and practicing the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, within the mind of equanimity, they shall perceive only sentient beings without conceptual discrimination, becoming like those in the state of non-conception; thus, I wish to cause them to practice wisdom within the mind of equanimity.

“By gathering in stinginess and greed, one gives rise to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); by transforming those who violate the precepts, one gives rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); by means of the dharma of non-self, one gives rise to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); by being detached from the marks of body and mind, one gives rise to the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); by means of the mark of bodhi, one gives rise to the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); and by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one gives rise to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).”
Previously, the four immeasurables were explained as the gift of Dharma; now, the six perfections are distinguished as the gift of Dharma.
When a bodhisattva initiates practice, each and every action possesses three intentions:
first, seeking the Buddha-way; second, delivering sentient beings; and third, not contravening the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, this text explains the six perfections through three pairs:
the first two involve breaking stinginess for the sake of others to give rise to *dāna* (generosity), and subduing transgressions to give rise to *śīla* (ethical discipline).
The following two use the two types of emptiness to give rise to the two practices:
Arising patience through the non-existence of self is the emptiness of persons;
abandoning the marks of body and mind and arising diligence is called the emptiness of dharmas.

The latter two are the bodhi of the two types of wisdom: one arises dhyāna because of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and next one arises prajñā because of the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).
Prajñā is true wisdom; therefore, one gives rise to Prajñā by means of the *sattva-prajñā* mind.
Furthermore, because Bodhi is the adornment of a Buddha’s merit, one gives rise to Dhyāna; because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the adornment of a Buddha’s wisdom, one gives rise to Prajñā.
Furthermore, bodhi is the mental activity of the Buddha; therefore, it was previously stated that quiescence is bodhi.
Thus, wisdom is the practice of *śamatha*, for when one gives rise to dhyāna, one abides in stillness.
Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the Buddha’s contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), he gives rise to Prajñā; Prajñā is contemplation.
"He gives rise to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in order to teach and transform sentient beings."
To prioritize sentient beings is to neglect the meaning of emptiness; to prioritize the meaning of emptiness is to abandon sentient beings.
One who thoroughly understands the characteristics of phenomena and leaves their mind empty of grasping will, throughout the day, transform sentient beings while never deviating from emptiness.
"Not abandoning conditioned phenomena while giving rise to the signless":
to manifest in accordance with transformation while existing within them is called "not abandoning the conditioned";
to know that existence is eternally quiescent is called "giving rise to the signless."
"Manifesting birth while giving rise to non-action":
appearing in forms according to circumstances is called manifesting birth;
knowing that birth is without birth is therefore called non-action.
“Exerting the power of skillful means to uphold the True Dharma.
Indeed, one who wishes to establish the True Dharma must employ skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).

“One should initiate the four methods of attraction (saṃgraha-vastu) to deliver sentient beings; initiate the method for removing arrogance by reverently serving all; initiate the three steadfast dharmas regarding body, life, and wealth; and initiate the dharma of mindfulness within the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti).”
The six recollections are the six recollections of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, generosity, ethical discipline, and the devas.
"One gives rise to a mind of straightforwardness toward the six points of reverent harmony."

Third, to perform the actions of body, speech, and mind with a compassionate heart; fourth, to share any significant gains or offerings received with others; fifth, to maintain pure precepts; and sixth, to cultivate the wisdom that brings about the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*).

Without a straightforward mind, one cannot possess the six qualities; without these six qualities, one cannot harmonize the multitude; and if the multitude is not harmonious, it is not the way of reverent obedience.
Benevolence of body, speech, and mind constitutes sameness of inner mind.

Sameness of precepts refers to the sameness of practice; sameness of view refers to the sameness of understanding; sameness of benefit refers to the sameness of material wealth; and sameness of practice and understanding refers to the sameness of the Dharma.

Furthermore, "common view" refers to the sameness of mind; "common precepts" refers to the sameness of body; "common benefit" provides for the sustenance of the body; and "common practice" is the external equipment beyond the mind.
Because the two assemblies formerly fell into discord and contention, the Buddha taught these six points of harmonious respect.
“Practicing wholesome dharmas gives rise to pure livelihood.
Whatever wholesome deeds one performs without a crooked mind constitutes right livelihood.
“Pure joy gives rise to drawing near to the noble ones; not harboring hatred for others gives rise to a mind of self-discipline.”
"Drawing near to the Sage, one gives rise to pure joy; seeing evil, one has no mind of aversion.
By means of the Dharma of renunciation, one arouses the profound mind.
Through renunciation, one is able to enter deeply into the Buddha-dharma and fully practice the pure precepts.
"One practices what has been taught to give rise to great learning; one dwells in secluded places by means of the dharma of non-contention.
Hostility and contention arise within the assembly, while non-contention emerges from seclusion."
"One approaches the Buddha-wisdom by engaging in profound meditation.
The Buddha-wisdom is deep and far-reaching; it cannot be approached without meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"One releases the bonds of sentient beings by arising on the stages of practice."
"If one does not cultivate one's own conduct, how can one liberate others?

One initiates the karma of merit by manifesting the primary and secondary marks and purifying the Buddha-fields; one initiates the karma of wisdom by knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma accordingly; and one initiates the karma of insight by knowing all phenomena without grasping or rejecting, entering the gate of the single characteristic."
The six perfections are broadly divided into two categories:
the first three constitute merit (puṇya), and the latter three constitute wisdom (prajñā).
When one possesses both merit and wisdom, it is like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird.
Each of these, merit and wisdom, is further divided into two.
Regarding the two aspects of the gate of merit:
first, it brings about internal marks and signs of excellence; second, it brings about the external pure land.
The two aspects of the opening of the gate of wisdom are:
illuminating existence is knowledge (*jñāna*), and discerning emptiness is wisdom (*prajñā*).
"It severs all afflictions, all obstructions, and all unwholesome dharmas, and gives rise to all wholesome karma."
To sever all afflictions means to eliminate the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); this is the function of wisdom.
All obstructions refer to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
All unwholesome dharmas and the arising of all wholesome karmas constitute the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
These two clarify the activities of merit and wisdom.
"By attaining all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to all factors conducive to the path of the Buddha" summarizes merit and wisdom once again.
"In this way, son of good family!
This is the assembly for the gift of Dharma.
If a bodhisattva dwells in this assembly for the gift of Dharma, they become a great donor and also a field of merit for all sentient beings."
One who initiates practice to benefit others is called a donor (*dānapati*);
one who is worthy of receiving offerings is thus termed a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
A person who practices the gift of Dharma possesses both virtues simultaneously; whereas one who practices the gift of material wealth is merely a donor and not a field of merit.
“World-Honored One!
When Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, two hundred people from among the assembly of brahmins all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, my mind attained purity; marvelling at such an unprecedented occurrence, I prostrated at Vimalakīrti’s feet and offered him a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, yet he was unwilling to accept it.”
From this point downward is the third section, clarifying the text on the benefits received.
That the items remain after seven days of giving indicates that they were most highly esteemed.
The preceding account of Vimalakīrti was intended to manifest his devotion to the gift of the Dharma.

Furthermore, Vimalakīrti knew that although [the donor] had renounced his wealth for seven days, it was because he had not yet exhausted his own attachments; therefore, he taught the gift of Dharma to cause him to relinquish what he held most precious.

Vimalakīrti refused to accept [the offerings], as his original intent was to preach the Dharma and censure material wealth, while also wishing to open the way for future impartial giving and to ensure that the donor’s sincerity was properly received. Thus, he did not accept them.
I said: "Householder!
I pray that you will certainly accept it; give it as you please."
Vimalakīrti then accepted the necklace, divided it into two parts, gave one part as a gift to the lowliest beggar in this assembly, and took the other part to offer to that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.

Although the preceding section demonstrated the gift of Dharma, it did not yet teach how to properly obtain the gift of material wealth; therefore, by extending the gift from the highest to the lowest, it clarifies that the mind of giving is impartial, thereby fulfilling the intention of properly obtaining the gift of material wealth.

The preceding section clarified that one obtains the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma through pure names; however, it did not yet clarify the mind that mobilizes these two gifts. Therefore, when giving extends from the highest to the lowest, it is called "mobilizing the mind of giving."
"The entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa in the land of Prabhāsa.

Because that Buddha’s majestic virtue was preeminent and his land was pure, [the text] first mentions the gift in order to inspire the assembly to generate a superior aspiration, and only thereafter allows them to behold it.
"Furthermore, he saw pearl necklaces above that Buddha transform into a jeweled pavilion with four pillars, its four sides exquisitely adorned yet not obstructing one another.
Such is the wondrous nature of the future retribution obtained through performing good deeds.
The precious terrace with four pillars represents the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) of the fruit of Buddhahood; it rises high above and covers below.
"Without obstruction" means that a single virtue does not obstruct any other virtue.
When Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he spoke as follows:

"If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar, regarding them as the very embodiment of the Tathāgata’s field of merit, without making distinctions and with equal great compassion, seeking no karmic reward—this is what is called the fulfillment of the gift of Dharma."
"The beggars within the city, having witnessed this supernatural power and heard what was said, all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This passage also describes the attainment of benefit.
"Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
This is the third conclusion regarding the inability [to visit].
The Sūtra clarifies that fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra) differ; as some say:
Giving to ordinary beings yields inferior retribution, while giving to noble ones yields superior retribution;
this is based on the relative thickness or thinness of the field [of merit], and thus the resulting blessings are few or many.
Now, when it is said that the honorable and the lowly share a single characteristic, two meanings may be understood:
First, because the Buddha is the supreme field of respect and sentient beings are the ultimate field of compassion, they are said to be "equal.
Second, because sentient beings and the Buddha are both identical to the true mark (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no duality between them.
In terms of giving with a mind of right contemplation, it is therefore equal.

As for the text stating that it is "equal to great compassion," following the intended meaning of Master Zhao’s commentary, it refers to the alignment of the noble and the humble within a single mark; because one gives by responding with a mind of impartial compassion, it is said to be "equal to great compassion."
Another interpretation is as follows:
"Great Compassion" refers to the Buddha.
Now, by bestowing [merit] upon lowly beggars so that they may equal the mark of the Buddha's Great Compassion, it is said that they "equal Great Compassion."

Although this is actually the gift of material wealth, it is called the "gift of Dharma" because it attains the contemplation of equality; since this is not within the capacity of the gift of material wealth, it is said that the gift of Dharma is fully perfected.

In this manner, each of those bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words of Vimalakīrti, and all declared, "We are unable to go to him to inquire after his illness."
These second thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas each declined, saying they were unable [to visit], though the text does not record their names in full.
**Chapter Five: Mañjuśrī Inquires After the Illness (4)** Regarding the purpose for the inclusion of this chapter, there are eight causes and conditions:

First, the "Chapter on the Disciples" concerns the minor path of the śrāvakas, while the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas" concerns those at the stage of the cause; therefore, both groups were unable to hear of the illness.
Mañjuśrī is capable of inquiring after the illness because he served as the attendant for the Buddhas of antiquity.

Second, the Supreme Person employs manifold strategies without fixed method; his traces of concealment and manifestation differ, and his long and short lives respond alternately to suit the dispositions of beings. Since the entrustment of awakening through spiritual capacity rests with Mañjuśrī, he goes to inquire after the illness.
Third, previously the Buddha commanded others to describe his past teachings, whereas now he commands Mañjuśrī to describe his present teaching.
Fourth, previously when those commanded were unable, the virtue of Vimalakīrti was manifested through them;
now, because those commanded are capable, Vimalakīrti manifests his own virtue himself.
Fifth, in the previous [state of] incapacity, he extensively elucidated the purity of name and wisdom;
now, because his life-force is capable, he fully manifests his supernormal powers and wisdom.
Sixth, in the previous incapacity, he destroyed three kinds of views—namely, those of ordinary beings, the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas.
Now, because Mañjuśrī was able to inquire, he has only now been able to enter the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvas.
Seventh: previously, because Mañjuśrī was unable to inquire, it clarified the relative status of the persons;
now, because Mañjuśrī was able to inquire, it reveals the wondrousness of the Dharma.
Eighth: From the preceding sections, the sequence of causes and conditions has been analyzed; from this chapter onward, the actual exposition is clarified.
Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies that he has already attained Buddhahood in the past, with the name Dragon-Seed Honored One (*Nāgagotra-guru*).

Among the fifty-three Buddhas, Mañjuśrī is the Buddha Joyful-Treasury-Maṇi-Jewel-Accumulation (*Ānandagarbha-maṇiratna-asaṃbhava*), who currently resides in the world of Constant Joy (*Sadāpramudita*) in this direction, manifesting as a wandering bodhisattva.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "He comes from the golden world of the Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna in the eastern direction," and it also says: "Mañjuśrī is the mother of immeasurable Buddhas."
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "He is the ninth-generation patriarch of Śākyamuni.
Following this passage, there are six chapters in total, which broadly open into two sections.
The first chapter briefly elucidates the two wisdoms;
the subsequent five chapters extensively elucidate the two wisdoms.
Within these chapters, there is further a twofold distinction:
First, the commissioning of Mañjuśrī to inquire after his illness; second, his acceptance of the commission.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
This was the first exhortation.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"That superior person is difficult to respond to.
This is the second time the receiving of the mandate is clarified.
According to the text, it consists of three parts:
This consists of three parts: first, the events prior to the inquiry after illness; second, the actual inquiry after illness; and third, the events following the inquiry after illness.
The first chapter is divided into two sections:
first, the explanation of receiving the command and coming forth; second, the clarification of arriving because of having come.
Each consists of four phrases.
Regarding the first chapter, there are four points:
first, it clarifies that he sets out because he wishes to receive [the Buddha's] life-force.
First, by extolling the virtues of Vimalakīrti, those who hear it will give rise to the thought that such a person is difficult to encounter;
second, he himself receives the command and departs;
third, the great assembly follows him.
Fourth, Mañjuśrī went together with the assembly;
this is the first chapter.
"Profoundly penetrating the true reality (*tathatā*)."
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is difficult to fathom; though the followers of the Two Vehicles have attained it, they have not exhausted its source, being like the rabbit and the horse.
The Great Being (*mahāsattva*) has perfectly realized its limits and depths, comparable to that king of horses.
"Skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
The former [phrase] praised his internal realization of the true nature of reality; now, this praises his external skill in preaching the Dharma.
This means he is adept at conveying manifold meanings through concise words, and it extols his excellence in grasping the essential tenor of the Dharma's exposition.
"His eloquence is unimpeded and his wisdom is unhindered.
His verbal eloquence responds perfectly and without obstruction, thereby accomplishing the supreme excellence of preaching the essential Dharma;
his wisdom is all-pervasive and without hindrance, thereby accomplishing the supreme depth of penetrating the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
"He possesses complete knowledge of all the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas and enters without exception into the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
To know the rituals of the bodhisattvas in their immediate proximity refers to understanding within one's own sphere;
to awaken to the secret treasury of all Buddhas from a distance refers to understanding beyond one's own sphere.
The three secrets of body, speech, and mind are called the "secret treasury.
"Subduing all māras" refers to the destruction of heterodoxy.
"Playing with supernormal powers" (yōxi shentong) clarifies the correct [state].
The transformations of supernormal powers constitute "play" (you);
Because he wishes to attract sentient beings, what is not real for him is called "play.
Furthermore, although his supernormal powers are great, those capable of them find them easy; since they pose no difficulty for him, they are like play.
Furthermore, he wanders through the realms to transform sentient beings, finding delight therein; thus it is called "play" (*līlā*).
"His wisdom and skillful means are both fully perfected.
Since the virtues of the Mahāsattva are inexhaustible, the sūtra concludes with these two types of knowledge at the end.
Wisdom refers to ultimate wisdom (*prajñā*), while skillful means refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*).
Because it exhausts the source of ultimate wisdom and reaches the very bottom of skillful means, it is called "crossing over" (*pāramitā*).
"Nevertheless, I shall now comply with the Buddha’s sacred command and go to him to inquire about his illness.
This was the second time he accepted the mission and departed.
His virtue is such that I am not fit to confront him.
"We shall proceed only after receiving your holy command.
Thereupon, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings among the assembly all thought to themselves:
"Now that these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, are conversing together, they will surely discourse upon the sublime Dharma."
"At that moment, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow him.
This was the third assembly that followed.
Since there is a supreme Sage, he must surely preach the wondrous Dharma; therefore, I lead [the disciples] with the desire to hear what has not been heard before.

Although the disciples are very numerous, only five hundred are mentioned because the remaining śrāvakas focus their minds solely on the cessation of suffering and do not seek the supreme Dharma, and thus they are not included in this enumeration.
These five hundred disciples have deeply penetrated wisdom and delight in hearing the supreme Dharma, which is why they travel together.

Furthermore, these five hundred were secretly bodhisattvas while outwardly appearing as śrāvakas; because [the Buddha] wished to censure the Small Vehicle and exalt the Great Vehicle, he singled them out for mention.
"Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the various bodhisattvas, the great assembly of disciples, and all the devas and humans, respectfully surrounded [him] and entered the great city of Vaiśālī."
This fourth passage describes Mañjuśrī’s actual departure.
Above, he accords with the Buddha’s intent; below, he benefits those with the karmic capacity. Therefore, he departs together with the assembly.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself:
"Now Mañjuśrī has arrived with a great assembly.
By means of his supernormal powers, he has vacated the interior of the room, removing all furnishings and attendants, leaving behind only a single couch upon which he lies ill."
This second section clarifies how one arrives without coming.
It also consists of four parts according to the text:
first, waiting for the guest in an empty room; second, Mañjuśrī’s silent reception; third, the householder’s inquiry; and fourth, Mañjuśrī’s response.
There are six general reasons for using an empty room to receive guests: first, to liken the room to the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata;

second, to desire to gather all sentient beings as attendants; third, to borrow the seat from King Dīpaṃkara; fourth, to answer the question regarding the manifestation of the form-body everywhere; fifth, to request food from the Fragrant Land; and sixth, because all various discourses on emptiness have always proceeded by means of this.
Furthermore, one may also give rise to the latter five categories:
when there is no empty seat, one gives rise to the "Inconceivable" chapter;
when there is no empty attendant, one gives rise to the "Contemplating Sentient Beings" chapter.
The manifestation of the heavenly maidens is the production of the "Chapter on the Buddha Path";
the emptiness of having no retinue is the production of the "Chapter on the Dharma Gate of Non-duality";
and the emptiness of having no food or drink is the production of the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation."
Question:
For what reason did he place only a single bed and lie down because of illness?
Answer:
The empty room illustrates the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-prajñā*), while lying ill illustrates the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Furthermore, the empty room serves to illustrate *prajñā*, while lying ill serves to illustrate great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Furthermore, the empty room possesses the six aforementioned meanings; his lying ill is intended to manifest the illness of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion as well as the illnesses of sentient beings’ ignorance and craving.
"When Mañjuśrī entered the house, he saw that the room was empty and devoid of all things, with [Vimalakīrti] alone upon a single bed."
This second passage is Mañjuśrī’s silent acceptance.

It is said that those who see it grasp its essential meaning; since the previous appearance of illness in the empty chamber manifested the two paths of emptiness and compassion, as well as the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, this current passage likewise accepts that same intent.
Then Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī!"
“He comes without the characteristic of coming; he sees without the characteristic of seeing.
This is the third consolation from Vimalakīrti.
Regarding the phrase “he comes without the characteristic of coming,” some say:
The Dharma-body has no coming, while the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) has a coming; therefore, it is said that "it comes with the characteristic of not coming.

Some say: in the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) there is no coming, while in the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) there is a coming; therefore, it is said that "it comes with the characteristic of not coming."
Some say: "Substantial dharmas have no coming;
it is their continuity that has coming. Others say: [Substantial dharmas have no coming; it is their continuity that has coming.]
The essence of the dharma-realm has no coming; the function of the dharma-realm has a coming. Some say:
the Middle Way has no coming, while conventional designations have a coming.

Now, to clarify this passage: it is not merely a case of the guest and host exchanging words of mutual consolation in the immediate context; rather, it reaches back to unify the entire sutra and encompasses all teachings. Therefore, these words were placed at the beginning of the chapter as a title, much like the phrase "dwelling in non-dwelling" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* or the principle of "hearing what is unheard" in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The reason for making this statement is that the assembly at the time believed Mañjuśrī had come from the Āmra grove and had met Vimalakīrti;
therefore, [the text] now clarifies that it was Mañjuśrī.
Coming is coming without having come; seeing is seeing without having seen. This distinguishes one from ordinary people and those of the two vehicles.
Because one is able to come without coming and see without seeing, this constitutes the ultimate excellence of goodness.
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so,
householder."
"If it has already come, it does not come again; if it has already gone, it does not go again. Why is this so?
That which comes comes from nowhere, and that which goes goes nowhere; what was once visible can no longer be seen."
This fourth response by Mañjuśrī fulfills the intent of Vimalakīrti.
As for the statement, "If he has already come, he does not come again," this clarifies the meaning that there is no coming throughout the three periods of time.
Since that which has come has already arrived and the matter of its arrival has already passed, there is no "coming.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that that which has gone does not go again: from the perspective of the Ānanda Garden looking toward the Abbot’s Quarters, one sees Mañjuśrī as having gone; from the perspective of the Abbot’s Quarters looking toward the Ānanda Garden, one sees Mañjuśrī as having come. Thus, the meaning of going and coming is clarified.
That "the coming one comes from nowhere" clarifies that the garden is empty;
that "the departing one goes nowhere" clarifies that the abbot’s quarters are empty.
Since it is thus with coming and going, it is likewise so with the perception of phenomena.
"Setting this matter aside for a moment.
Second, the actual clarification of the inquiry regarding illness.
This section is divided into two parts according to the text:
First, a request to suspend the digression; second, the formal inquiry regarding the illness.

Although "not coming yet coming" and "not seeing yet seeing" constitute the fundamental tenet of this transformative master, these expressions differ from the specific discourse on the illness; since the Sage’s intent has not yet been fully proclaimed, it is appropriate to cease the digression.
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder, can you endure your illness?
This marks the second section, which clearly presents the inquiry regarding the illness.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the illness of the layperson is explained; second, the illnesses of sentient beings are distinguished.
These two are also the two types of illnesses: that of the bodhisattva of profound practice and that of the person who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment].
The first chapter has three sections:
first, a discussion on the nature of illness; second, a discussion on the empty room; and third, a discussion on the characteristics of illness.
Regarding the first section, there is first the question and then the answer.
There are two intentions in this inquiry:
first, to respectfully recount the Buddha’s questions; second, to pose one's own questions.
Regarding the first, there are three questions:

Regarding the previous inquiry into the severity of the illness: that which can be endured is considered light, while that which cannot be endured is considered heavy; therefore, he asked, "Can you endure it?
[The response was: "There is some improvement from the treatment."
This second question concerns the harm caused by the failure to apply remedies.
"Will it not increase?"— this third question concerns the increase resulting from the failure to apply remedies.
“The World-Honored One sends his most earnest greetings of immeasurable concern.
This generally conveys the Sage’s intention, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one.
“Householder, what is the cause from which this illness arises?”
In this second passage, Mañjuśrī himself poses a question, which likewise consists of three parts.
First, he asks about the cause of the illness: by what cause did he contract the disease?
"How long has it been since he fell ill?
This question concerns the duration since the onset of the illness.
"How shall it be extinguished? [This asks] how it will cease.
This question addresses the remedy: "When can this illness be extinguished?
Vimalakīrti replied, "From ignorance and craving, my illness arises."
This is the second response to the questions.
Although there were six questions above, only the last three are answered, while the first three are addressed by implication.

For instance, the answers to the questions regarding the cause of illness and its long duration implicitly answer the initial questions concerning the severity of the illness and its subsequent increase.
If one answers the question regarding the cessation of illness, it simultaneously answers the second question concerning the impairment by illness.

Regarding the answers to the latter three questions, they constitute three distinct parts; however, their sequence differs: first, the answer to the second question on long duration; next, the answer to the third question on the cessation of illness; and finally, the answer to the first question on the cause of illness.
Regarding the statement, "From ignorance and craving, my illness arises": because sentient beings give rise to craving due to ignorance, they receive a body because of that craving;
because there is a body, there is illness. Out of compassion for their illness, the Bodhisattva likewise has illness.

The illnesses of sentient beings have existed since beginningless time; because the Bodhisattva feels compassion for sentient beings, he too gives rise to illness, and thus his illness is likewise long-standing.
"Because all sentient beings are ill, therefore I am ill;
when the illnesses of all sentient beings are extinguished, then my illness is extinguished."
This answers the third question regarding the cessation of illness, consisting of the principle, the analogy, and the application.
The illness of a Bodhisattva arises for the sake of sentient beings;
once that [others'] illness is extinguished, then my own illness is also extinguished.
"Why is this? It is because one enters into birth-and-death for the sake of sentient beings; where there is birth-and-death, there is illness.
If sentient beings can become free from illness, then the Bodhisattva will no longer have illness."
The Dharma-body is without birth; how much more so does it possess form?
Since it has no form, from what cause could illness arise?
Nevertheless, because it undergoes birth for the sake of others, it cannot be without form.
Since it possesses form, it cannot be without illness.
If that [form] were free from illness, the Bodhisattva would likewise have no further illness.
"It is like an elder who has only one son; when the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill."
"If a child’s illness is cured, the parents are also cured.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva loves all sentient beings as his own children; when sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is ill, and when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the Bodhisattva is also cured."
This provides both the analogy and its application to answer the preceding question regarding the cessation of illness.
Furthermore, the statement "From what cause does this illness arise? answers the first question.
The question was originally presented first, while the answer now follows later; hence the use of the term "furthermore" (*yòu*).

As for not answering first: once the arising and ceasing of the afflictions, as well as their duration and proximity, have been clarified, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) will manifest of itself. Therefore, the former response addressed arising and ceasing, while the latter response addressed great compassion.
"The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion.
Before [enlightenment], the bodhisattva’s compassion is inexhaustible, yet it arises together with delusion and craving;
after [enlightenment], their compassion is endless, yet it perishes along with all living beings.
The source of the sicknesses of sentient beings arises from ignorance and craving, whereas the root of the Bodhisattva’s illness is born of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Question:
Since the cause of the Bodhisattva’s illness arises because of sentient beings, how can it be said to arise from great compassion?
Answer:
Because sentient beings possess great compassion, and because the Bodhisattva’s mind is imbued with compassion, the Bodhisattva’s body may suffer illness. Mañjuśrī said:
"Layman! Why is this room empty and devoid of attendants?
This second [question] discusses the emptiness of the room.
First, the Pure Name clarifies that the room is empty, and only then does it indicate the illness;
this clarity arises from emptiness, thereby demonstrating that compassion gives rise to skillful means—that is, true wisdom generates expedient methods.

When Mañjuśrī first inquires about the illness of Great Compassion and subsequently asks about the empty room, he demonstrates that Great Compassion is itself emptiness; because this also proceeds from skillful means, it clarifies true wisdom.
At the beginning, there are two questions:
the first concerns the empty room.
A lady’s residence should contain articles of daily necessity, yet now it is vast and entirely empty; for what reason is this so?
Furthermore, as a general rule, those who are ill must necessarily have attendants; for what reason are there none?
The reason for asking about these two matters together is that both are absent, and thus they are asked in conjunction.
The question regarding the empty room clarifies the non-existence of dharmas;
the question regarding the absence of an attendant reveals the non-existence of persons. Vimalakīrti said:
"The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty.
This response to the two questions constitutes two distinct parts.
The answer to the first question consists of two sections.
The Way of equality is such that its principle is non-dual; there are no lands throughout the ten directions that are not empty. Why, then, do you ask about the emptiness of a single room?

As for your citing the Buddha-lands, the deluded might say that while the fruits upon which sentient beings depend are illusory and thus can be empty, the Buddha-lands are real and therefore cannot be empty.
Furthermore, because sentient beings lack the power of sustenance, their realm may be empty; however, since the Buddha possesses the power of sustenance, his realm should not be empty.
Thus, it is now clarified that even though the Buddha has attained mastery, he cannot cause his own land to become "existent," let alone the lands of sentient beings.
He asked again:
"By what means is it empty?
"Your room is empty because it lacks objects; yet, since the Buddha-lands of the ten directions appear therein in their full reality, how can it be considered empty?"
The answer says:
"By means of the emptiness of emptiness.
Here, "above-emptiness" refers to the emptiness of the wisdom of emptiness.
"Lower emptiness" refers to the emptiness of external objects.
One must observe them with the wisdom of emptiness; only then will all things be empty. This emptiness does not mean that they are empty because they are non-existent entities.
He asked again:
"For what purpose is emptiness empty?
Since phenomena are fundamentally empty by nature, for what purpose does the wisdom of emptiness further empty all phenomena?
The answer is:
"It is empty because of the dharma of non-discriminative emptiness.
Although dharmas are empty by their own nature, they must necessarily rely upon the wisdom of emptiness.
If there were no wisdom of emptiness, then the self would exist.
By employing this non-conceptual wisdom of emptiness, one attains emptiness;
having attained emptiness, the self no longer exists.

The reason it is called "non-conceptualizing wisdom of emptiness" is that the arising of ignorance originates from conceptualization; yet, because all phenomena are signless, wisdom is without conceptualization.
Therefore, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explicitly identifies the wisdom of emptiness as non-conceptual wisdom.
Furthermore, it asks:
"Can emptiness be conceptually differentiated?
From the preceding section upward, the emptiness of external objects has been clarified; from this point downward, the emptiness of wisdom is to be distinguished.
Since the wisdom that realizes the essence of emptiness does not engage in conceptual differentiation, one thereby knows that all phenomena are empty.
"Can the essence of this very wisdom that is capable of contemplation be differentiated as being existent?
He replied:
"Differentiation, too, is empty."
This clarifies that the wisdom of emptiness is itself empty.

If wisdom were different from emptiness, it would constitute conceptual discrimination; because wisdom is also empty, there is no discrimination. Therefore, it is said that "discrimination is also empty."
He asked again:
"Where should emptiness be sought?

Previously, based on correct contemplation, emptiness was clarified; however, those who are deluded might think that the meaning of emptiness resides in the correct and not in the erroneous. Therefore, he asks where the meaning of emptiness lies in order to clarify that the erroneous and the correct are non-dual.
The answer says:
"One should seek it within the sixty-two views.
Since the sixty-two views are themselves ultimate emptiness, one uses these views to clarify the locus of emptiness.
He asked again:
"Where should the sixty-two views be sought?
Previously, he had merged the heterodox and the orthodox; now, having brought together bondage and liberation, he asks where all these views should be sought.
The answer is:
"One should seek it within the liberation of all Buddhas.
Since the liberation of all Buddhas is ultimate emptiness, it is non-dual with all views; therefore, one seeks all views within liberation.
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?
This question was posed to clarify that sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual.
The answer is:
"One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings.

Those who are deluded claim that the liberation of the Buddhas resides in correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), while the mental activities of sentient beings dwell amidst the afflictions of craving and false views. To clarify this, it is shown that sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally without two distinct characteristics; craving and false views are themselves Great Nirvāṇa. Therefore, one seeks the liberation of the Buddhas within the mental activities of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, regarding what you asked:
'Why do you have no attendant?'— all Māras and all non-Buddhists are my attendants."
This answers the second question.
Previously, the empty room was explained to manifest emptiness; now, the absence of attendants is explained to manifest existence.
The reason for this is that because of the empty room, all things within the Buddha-land above are subsumed as empty; [whereas] by the absence of attendants, existence is manifested.
Because there is no attendant, he gathers the multitudes of living beings below to serve as his attendants.
Furthermore, while the previous section clarified the empty chamber to distinguish the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*),
the present discussion on the absence of an attendant clarifies the existence of persons (*pudgala*).

The emptiness of phenomena refers to the wisdom of reality (*prajñā*), while the existence of persons refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya*); therefore, this sutra contains these two forms of wisdom from beginning to end. Why is this so?
"The various Māras delight in birth and death, yet the Bodhisattva does not abandon birth and death;
the non-Buddhists delight in various views, yet the Bodhisattva is unshaken by those views."
Māras delight in the five sensual desires and do not seek transcendence from the world; therefore, it is said they "delight in birth and death.
Although non-Buddhists seek transcendence from the world, they cling to their own doctrines; therefore, it is said they "delight in various views."
Through great compassion, one contemplates birth-and-death as identical to nirvana, and thus is able not to abandon it;
one contemplates all views as identical to right view, and thus is able to remain unmoved.
Because one is neither moved nor abandons, one is able to attain the status of an attendant.
Question:
Without moving or abandoning [the object], how does one serve?
Answer:
To be neither moving nor abandoning is to attain right contemplation; having attained right contemplation, one nourishes the Dharma-body, thereby acting as its attendant.
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder, what are the characteristics of your illness?"
This is the third discussion concerning the characteristics of illness.

This discussion of the characteristics of illness should logically have occurred prior to the inquiry regarding the empty room; however, [the author] now wishes to demonstrate the mutual clarification between emptiness and existence.

Having first explained the existence of illness and subsequently analyzed the empty room, [the author] now intends to use the empty room as an analogy to show that the illness is likewise empty; therefore, the inquiry into the characteristics of illness follows after the discussion of the empty room.
Observing this matter, it appears as if there were no illness, yet you say there is an illness; since I have not seen its characteristics, I ask about it.
Furthermore, each of the four hundred and four illnesses has its own specific characteristics; what are the characteristics of the illness of Great Compassion?
Therefore, he asked him. Vimalakīrti replied,
"My illness is formless and invisible."

Great compassion is without conditions, yet there is nothing it does not take as its object; because there is nothing it does not take as its object, it manifests illness in accordance with sentient beings.

It likewise manifests forms in accordance with sentient beings. Since it is without conditions, this clarifies that I am without illness; if one is without illness, how could there be the possession of forms?
Furthermore, another interpretation is this:
because he manifests illness in accordance with the needs of sentient beings, he resorts to the sick quarters;
yet, because this has no substantial reality, it is called "formless."
He asked again:
"Is this illness joined with the body, or is it joined with the mind?
Those who are deluded, hearing that the illness cannot be seen, will assume that the illness of the mind is formless; because it is joined with the mind, it cannot be seen.
Someone may say: "The body's illness is subtle; because it still conforms to the body, it cannot be seen. Therefore, I ask: do the mind and body conjoin? He replied:
"It is not a conjunction with the body, for the characteristics of the body are detached."
"Nor is it joined with the mind, for the mind is like an illusion.
"The body is detached from its marks" clarifies that the body is empty; "detached" is another name for emptiness.
"The mind is like an illusion" clarifies that the mind is empty.
The body is a physical form, which is why it is said to be "separate.
The mind moves without fixed direction, hence it is called an "illusion.
Since neither body nor mind exists, with whom would the illness conjoin?
Because they do not combine, they cannot be seen.
[The Buddha] was asked again:
"Regarding the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element—among these four great elements, which one is afflicted by disease?"

The body and mind are fundamentally composed of the combination of the four great elements; while the body and mind may be absent, the four great elements may still exist. Since the four hundred and four illnesses arise from these four great elements, which of them is the illness now?
Kumārajīva said: "The non-Buddhists speak only of the three great elements causing illness, but do not mention the earth element.

In the Buddha-dharma, it is fully explained that illness arises from the four great elements; thus, when one element is out of harmony, there are one hundred and one illnesses. When the four elements are discussed collectively, there are four types of illness."
He replied: "This illness is not the earth element, yet it is not separate from the earth element; it is likewise with the water, fire, and wind elements.
If the illness were identical to the four great elements, then there would have to be illness wherever each of the four great elements resides individually.
If the four great elements were each situated in their own separate locations, there would be no illness; therefore, we know they are not identical.
If illness existed apart from the four great elements, then when the four great elements are combined, there should be no illness.
Yet when the four great elements assemble, illness consequently arises; thus we know they are not separate.
Since they are neither identical nor separate, being a provisional confluence of causes and conditions, one knows that the illness is empty.
"The illnesses of sentient beings arise from the four great elements;
because they have illness, I am ill.

The Bodhisattva’s illness and the illnesses of sentient beings are neither identical nor separate. However, while the illnesses of sentient beings arise from the four great elements, the Bodhisattva’s illness arises from sentient beings; it does not arise from an actual conflict with the four great elements.
"At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
'How should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva?
This second section clarifies the sickness of sentient beings, which refers to bodhisattvas who have only recently begun their practice."
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, explaining consolation; second, distinguishing subduing.
As for consolation, it refers to comforting and instructing those who are ill by means of those who are currently free from illness.
Regarding the subduing of those who are afflicted by illness, one must first subdue one's own mind.

Since a practitioner at the initial stage of the path has already received this body and is further entangled in the suffering of disease, they will cling to life and fear death; thus, they increase the cycle of birth and death and fail to practice right contemplation. Therefore, one should provide instruction and consolation, enabling them to dwell within their illness while practicing self-transformation and transforming others.
Furthermore, regarding those who are afflicted by illness, as they possess mental afflictions, they must practice self-discipline.
Moreover, one should console and encourage them to accumulate merit, and through discipline, lead them away from evil.
Furthermore, one consoles and encourages them to practice with effortful cultivation (*sābhisaṃskāra-prayoga*), and through subduing them, causes them to realize emptiness and attain liberation.

As for the classification by stages: "consoling" refers to those prior to the thirty minds of the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), while "subduing" pertains to those within the internal ordinary beings from the thirty minds onward.
The preceding section distinguished the illness of Vimalakīrti as pertaining to those from the first bhūmi up to the Buddha; therefore, this chapter fully elucidates all worthy ones and sages.
First, he respectfully receives the previous question; next, he provides the answer.
However, there are three reasons why Mañjuśrī himself should offer words of consolation to the sick person, yet instead inquire of Vimalakīrti:
first, so that the assembly may focus their attention on the matter at hand;
second, so as to verify the patient’s testimony and thereby ascertain the true nature of the consolation offered; and third, [to demonstrate]... [text truncated].
Third, those who are fundamentally free from illness are able to offer consolation and encouragement.
Although Vimalakīrti manifests illness, he is in reality without illness; therefore, he is able to offer consolation and encouragement.
Vimalakīrti said: "One speaks of the impermanence of the body, but does not speak of wearying of or seeking liberation from the body.
This response regarding the internal [self] is divided into three parts:
First is the direct answer, followed by the summary.
The direct answer is twofold:
first, consolation is explained in terms of the gate of practice; second, consolation is explained in terms of the gate of vows.

The section on the practice of consolation clarifies the practice of providing comfort. First, it addresses the practice regarding what is to be abandoned; second, it clarifies the practice regarding what is attained.

Since there are many ways to provide consolation, for ordinary people who are bound by all fetters and who fear death because of their greed, one cannot preach impermanence; rather, one should simply protect their feelings by saying that they will soon recover from their illness.
If one were to console those who are śrāvakas, one would preach impermanence for them, so that they might swiftly sever their afflictions and enter nirvāṇa early.
Now, this passage consoles and exhorts bodhisattvas, causing them to transcend both the ordinary and the holy, and to practice self-cultivation while transforming others.
To speak of the impermanence of the body is to destroy the perversion of permanence and thereby distinguish oneself from ordinary people.
Ordinary people are greedily attached to this body; they cherish life and fear death, and fail to contemplate impermanence. Therefore, [the Buddha] does not speak of impermanence to them.
Now, those who have only just begun to practice know that the body must inevitably perish; how could they possibly harbor greed for it?
One who does not speak of wearying detachment from the body is one who has shattered the delusion of permanence, distinguishing them from those of the Two Vehicles.

The followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate the body as impermanent and consequently become weary of it, desiring to enter nirvana; therefore, one who now establishes oneself in illness to transform others should not seek to realize the fruits of the Two Vehicles.
"It is said that the body has suffering, yet it is not said that there is pleasure in nirvāṇa.
It is said that the body is without self, yet it speaks of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
It is said that the body is empty and quiescent, yet it does not speak of ultimate extinction."
There may be those who, though they hear of impermanence, still claim it is not suffering; for them, one preaches suffering.
There may be those who, though they hear of suffering, still claim that suffering and pleasure have a master; for them, one preaches emptiness and non-self.
For example, a great tree cannot be toppled by a single blow from an axe.
Since its roots have accumulated deeply, it cannot be extinguished by a single dharma; therefore, the four types of impermanence are fully explained.
Although they perceive the suffering of the body, they do not delight in the bliss of nirvana.
Although they know there is no self, they do not abandon their instruction of sentient beings because of that emptiness.
Although they understand the emptiness of the body, they do not grasp at the ultimate emptiness of nirvana.
Therefore, he is able to dwell securely within birth and death, sharing the same afflictions as all living beings.
Thus, by comforting and exhorting them, he causes them to recognize what ought to be practiced and what ought not to be practiced.
"To speak of repentance for the absence of offense, yet not speak of entering the past.
Previously, the Bodhisattva practice was taught for those of sharp faculties; now, the Dharma is further explained for those of dull faculties who have not yet attained realization.
Furthermore, previously, in refuting the eight inversions, consolation was explained by way of the departure from afflictions;
now, consolation is explained by way of the departure from karma.
Since today’s illness must necessarily stem from prior transgressions, he causes him to repent; thus it is said, "he speaks of repenting for prior transgressions."

Since it has already been stated that there is a prior offense, it would seem that karma possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that passes from the future to the present and from the present into the past; therefore, we now clarify that it does not enter the past.
"One does not enter the past because the nature of sin is empty; thus, there is no sin to be repented of or entered into.
Next, one takes pity on the illnesses of others by means of one's own illness."
Previously, consolation was provided by way of the gates of affliction and karma;
now, consolation is clarified by way of the gate of the retribution of suffering, so as to lead one to reflect upon oneself and feel compassion for others.
I am now slightly ill, yet my suffering is already such as this; how much more so for the sentient beings in the evil realms who endure immeasurable suffering?
Furthermore, though I possess wisdom, I still suffer from this chronic ailment; how much more so for those who lack understanding?

To extend one's own compassion to others is the magnanimous resolve of a Great Being to provide universal succor; therefore, upon hearing this Dharma, one should neither cling to life nor fear death, but should properly practice it oneself and transform others.
"One should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in past lives and one should resolve to benefit all sentient beings.

Having endured immeasurable suffering throughout countless kalpas, this present suffering is but a moment; why should it cause such anxiety? One should simply exert oneself to rescue others from their suffering.
"Recall the merit one has cultivated.

According to the customs of foreign lands, every meritorious deed performed from birth until death is recorded individually; at the time of death, these are recited by those nearby so that the dying person may rely upon their merit and their mind will be free from sorrow and fear.
"Be mindful of pure livelihood.
Reflecting for oneself that from birth until the end one has always practiced right livelihood, one will certainly reach a happy destination; why, then, should one have any anxiety?
Furthermore, do not commit various unwholesome deeds to save yourself from physical illness, even at the cost of your life.
"Do not give rise to anxiety and distress.

The sick person has much anxiety; because of this excessive anxiety, distress arises. Therefore, it is clarified that there is no benefit in following anxiety, as it only leads pointlessly to distress.
"Always arouse diligence.
Because they are prone to indolence when ill, he exhorts them to be diligent, so that even if their bodies perish and their lives end, they do not abandon their resolve.
"One should act as a King of Physicians to cure all ailments.
Previously, consolation was explained by way of the gate of practice;
now, consolation is explained by way of the gate of aspiration, so that through this illness one may give rise to the great vow to act as a King of Physicians to cure all ailments of body and mind.
“A bodhisattva should console a sick bodhisattva in this way, causing them to rejoice.
This is the summary. Mañjuśrī said:
"Layman! How should a sick bodhisattva discipline his mind?
This second [section] clarifies discipline.

When there is skillful analogy externally and virtuous self-discipline internally, one can traverse the cycle of birth and death alongside all sentient beings, sharing their afflictions; though experiencing every kind of bitterness and hardship, one does not regard them as suffering.
This is precisely the meaning behind Vimalakīrti manifesting illness.
First there is the question, followed by the answer.

As for "subduing" (*vinaya*): the mind is like a galloping horse that is difficult to restrain; therefore, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one first disciplines it and subsequently subdues it.
Now, in order to clarify the method of subduing [the afflictions], he asks this question first. Vimalakīrti said:
"A bodhisattva who is ill should form this thought:"
"This present illness of mine arises entirely from the delusions, inversions, and various afflictions of past lives; it has no substantial reality. Who, then, is there to suffer this illness?
This is the second answer.
The textual exposition consists of three parts:

first, an explanation of self-cultivation and the taming of others; second, an explanation of the gains and losses associated with self-cultivation and the taming of others; third, an explanation that neither being tamed nor not being tamed is what constitutes true taming.
The initial section also has three parts:
first, self-discipline, which is actual wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*);
second, disciplining others, which refers to expedient wisdom (*upāyaprajñā*).
The third is the unification of clarity for the sake of self-cultivation and the transformation of others through subduing; this is the unification of the two types of wisdom.
The first section has three parts:
first, the emptiness of sentient beings; second, the emptiness of all phenomena; third, the emptiness of even the illness of emptiness.
By means of these three gates, one disciplines and subdues the mind.
The first section consists of four sentences:
first, using the future to illustrate the fundamental.
Now that suffering exists, one investigates its origin: suffering arises from illness; illness arises from the body; and the body arises from delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Since delusive conceptualization is not real, the body is likewise not real.
Since the body is not real, how could suffering be real?
"Why is this so? Because the four great elements combine, they are conventionally designated as a 'body. Since the four great elements have no master, the body likewise has no self."
This second phrase uses the fundamental to illustrate the derivative.
Previously, one inferred the absence of self by examining successive lifetimes; now, one infers the absence of self by examining the present lifetime.
Furthermore, previously one examined the cause of the body; now, one examines that the four great elements are the conditions for the body, and thus both are devoid of self.

One perceives only the four great elements and does not perceive a single master. If there were a master, there would necessarily be a self; however, since this is not the case, we know there is no master.
The four great elements are the basis of the body; if that basis has no master, how could the body, which is merely its derivative, possess a self?
"Furthermore, the arising of this illness is entirely due to attachment to a self; therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward a self.
This third phrase reveals its fault.
Generally speaking, there are two ways in which illness arises:
First, due to attachment to a self in past lives, one fully generates fetters and karma; the retribution of these fetters and karma results in the experience of suffering in the present.
Second, due to attachment to a self in the present, the mind is afflicted; when the mind is afflicted, illness increases.
"Once the root of the disease is known, one immediately eliminates the notion of a self (*ātman*) and the notion of sentient beings (*sattva*).
The fourth phrase concludes the elimination of the self.
Master Kumārajīva said: "That which is the root of the disease is what is called the 'self'."
Master Sengzhao said: "The 'self' that is fundamental is precisely the aforementioned delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because of the existence of delusive conceptualization, one perceives a self and sentient beings;
if one awakens to the fact that delusive conceptualization is a perversion, then there is neither self nor sentient beings."
"One should give rise to the conceptualization of dharmas.
From the preceding section upward, "non-self" was repeatedly investigated; from this point onward, the self is refuted by means of provisional dharmas.
Although [the conceptualization of dharmas] acts as a malady with respect to emptiness, it serves as a medicine with respect to the self; therefore, one borrows dharmas to eliminate the self.
"One should form this thought:
'This body is merely composed of a multitude of dharmas; its arising is solely the arising of dharmas, and its ceasing is solely the ceasing of dharmas.
This explains the perception of dharmas (*dharmasaṃjñā*).

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and all phenomena (*dharma*) conventionally assemble to form the body; their arising is solely the simultaneous arising of these phenomena, and their cessation is solely the simultaneous cessation of these phenomena. There is no separate, real sovereign that presides over their arising and cessation.
Having eliminated the notion of a self, one perceives only the dharmas of dependent origination; therefore, it is called the "notion of dharmas.
Furthermore, these dharmas do not know one another: when they arise, they do not say, "I am arising," and when they cease, they do not say, "I am ceasing."
The preceding phrase clarifies that there are only dharmas; this phrase distinguishes that they do not arise from a person.
Since all dharmas exist when conditions converge and disperse when conditions diverge, and their aggregation and dispersion occur without prior intention, dharmas are mutually unaware of one another.
"The sick bodhisattva, in order to eliminate the notion of dharmas, should form this thought:
'This notion of dharmas is itself a perversion.
Perversion is a great affliction; I should abandon it.'"
Below this, for the second time, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is distinguished.

Previously, phenomena were employed as a means to eliminate the self; these phenomena served as medicine for the self but are themselves a malady for emptiness. Therefore, they are eliminated, not because there are truly existent phenomena that must be removed.
Because of inversion, phenomena exist; therefore, one must depart from them.
"How does one depart loftily?
By departing from 'self' and 'what belongs to self.'"
I am the "inner" [self], and all phenomena external to me are my possessions.
Possessions are phenomena that exist in relation to a self;
since the self no longer exists, how could possessions exist independently?
“What is meant by being detached from ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self’?
It means to be detached from these two things: namely, not to dwell upon internal or external phenomena, but to practice equanimity.
Here, “internal” refers to the self, and “external” refers to all phenomena; these constitute the duality of relative opposition.
This means that by not dwelling on [distinctions], one acts with equanimity; therefore, it is called "detachment.
What is equanimity?
It is the equality of the self and nirvana.
The "self" is the most lowly of beings;
Nirvana is the supreme Dharma.
To view the supreme and the lowly as identical is called equality.
"Why is this so? Both 'self' and 'nirvāṇa' are empty.
By what are they empty?"
They are empty merely by virtue of being names. These two dharmas lack any fixed nature.

Because one turns away from nirvana, it is called "self"; because one abandons the self, it is called "nirvana. When these two dharmas exist in mutual dependence, then names arise. Since they have names only through mutual dependence, they lack fixedness; therefore, they are empty.
"Having attained this equanimity, there is no other illness remaining, only the illness of emptiness, and even the illness of emptiness is empty.
This third [point] clarifies that even the illness of emptiness is empty.

Since beginningless time, one has shattered existence to clarify emptiness; yet once existence is no longer established, emptiness likewise has no basis. To say that it is neither empty nor existent is what is called "right contemplation.
Thus, this sick bodhisattva accepts all sensations through non-acceptance; although he has not yet perfected the Buddha-dharma, he does not extinguish sensation to realize realization.
Below this, the second section clarifies the transformation and subduing of others.
This section also has three parts:
first, clarifying taking birth for the sake of sentient beings; second, clarifying enduring suffering for the sake of sentient beings; and third, removing the illnesses of sentient beings.
That which has nothing received is itself empty; even the sickness of emptiness is empty. Therefore, the mind does not receive or cling to either emptiness or existence.
As for the experiencing of various sensations, although the mind has nothing received, it undergoes birth as a being and experiences the suffering and pleasure within that birth.
It is held that when sentient beings undergo birth, they fully practice all deeds; this is called the Buddha-dharma.
If one has not yet fulfilled these various practices, one will not extinguish the three types of sensation and instead attain the nirvana of the two vehicles.
"If you experience suffering in your own person, you should contemplate the sentient beings of the evil realms and give rise to great compassion.
Having disciplined yourself, you should likewise discipline all sentient beings."
This second section further clarifies the endurance of suffering for the sake of sentient beings.

Since even my own body, endowed with merit and wisdom, still experiences such pain, how much more so must it be for the beings in the evil realms who undergo immeasurable suffering? Therefore, compassion arises.
"Since I have already disciplined myself through the three emptinesses, I must likewise discipline all beings.
One merely removes the illness without removing the dharma," he said,
for he intended to seek out the source of the affliction within things.
In the previous explanation of the meaning of "severing," it was shown that the Bodhisattva personally severs the three maladies of self, emptiness, and so forth.

Now, regarding the necessity of further severing the three maladies of sentient beings: in reality, there are no three dharmas to be removed; one merely removes the conceptualization of emptiness as being a malady.

It is like seeing flowers in the sky due to an eye disease; once the eye disease is cured, there is no "flower-in-the-sky" phenomenon to be removed, which is why it is said that "no phenomena are removed.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, "not removing" means merely destroying the sentient beings' illness of clinging to the existence of a self-nature (*svabhāva*), while not removing phenomena that are conventionally designated based on causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One merely severs attachment to grasping, but does not sever the view of self.
This 'view of self' is precisely the Buddha-nature.
Each of these two [positions] has its own specific meaning; it is not that there are no two interpretations.
"To teach for the sake of severing the root of illness.
This third section clearly explains teaching for the sake of severing the illnesses of sentient beings.
First, the two topical headings—the root of illness and teaching—were presented; next, these two headings are explained.
This is the initial heading.
"What is called the root of illness?
It is the presence of objective grasping (*ālambana*)."
"To have an object of attachment is the root of illness.
What is the object of attachment?
It is called the three realms."
This is the introductory section explaining illness.
Previously, it was taught that the Bodhisattva seeks the root of his own illness and settles his mind through principle; thus, he can abide in sickness without anxiety.
Now, it is clarified that for the sake of severing the illnesses of sentient beings, he investigates the origins of their diseases and subsequently responds to what is appropriate for them.

When the spirit is subtly stirred by a sign, the mind has something to which it is attached; that the mind has something to which it is attached is called "grasping at conditions" (*ālambana*). Grasping at conditions and seizing upon signs is the beginning of deluded thought and the root of all illness.

Once deluded thoughts take objects as their conditions, beauty and ugliness are distinguished; once beauty and ugliness are distinguished, hatred and love blaze forth together. Thus, myriad fetters are vexed within, and ten thousand ailments arise without.
The mind that is able to perceive is itself a false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and the objects perceived do not transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*).

The reason for this is that what lies beyond the triple world is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), whereas the mind of false conceptualization is characterized by grasping; therefore, it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted, and thus belongs to the triple world.
"How does one sever objective referents?
By means of non-apprehension.
If there is no apprehension, then there are no objective referents."
What is meant by "non-apprehension"?
It means being free from the two views.
What are the two views?
"This means that internal views and external views are non-apprehendable.
This explains the primary section on severing the sickness through instruction.
Since the root of the sickness consists of apprehending existence, the severance of the sickness consists of non-apprehension.
"Non-attainment" means that the mind does not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*).

If the mind were to grasp at any phenomena, then the mind would give rise to something; if the mind gives rise to something, then the mind becomes bound. One would thus be unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
If the mind has nothing to be apprehended, then the mind is not bound; thus, one attains liberation from birth, old age, and sickness.

That which is called "non-apprehension" refers to the non-attainment of the two views of internal and external, which is termed non-apprehension; it does not mean that there is some separate entity called non-apprehension. Therefore, it is said that the view of the internal and the view of the external are themselves non-apprehension.
Regarding "internal and external": internally there are deluded thoughts, and externally there are all phenomena; these are called the internal and external. "Mañjuśrī!
This is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind in order to sever the suffering of old age, sickness, and death."
"This is the bodhi of the Bodhisattva.
If it were not thus, that which has been cultivated and purified would be of no benefit.
This third section clarifies, in combination, the self-cultivation and the taming of others; it contains the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
