Because one is able to sever the root of illness for both oneself and others as described above, this is precisely the disciplining of the minds of both self and others.
Once the root of illness is severed, then old age, sickness, and death are eliminated.
Because it simultaneously severs [the afflictions] of both self and others, this is the bodhi of a Bodhisattva, which differs from that of the two vehicles.

The reason for speaking universally of *bodhi* is that *bodhi* takes actual benefit as its path; if one simultaneously achieves the severance [of afflictions] for both oneself and others, one attains quiescent contemplation, and thus is able to provide actual benefit.
If it were not so, there would be no benefit for oneself and no kindness toward others.
This is illustrated by the analogy: "Only by conquering one's enemies can one be called brave.
This is the explanation of the parable.
Old age, sickness, death, and so forth are enemies of the bodhisattva, and they are also enemies of sentient beings.

Furthermore, the enemies of sentient beings are themselves the enemies of the bodhisattva; for the bodhisattva regards all things as his own children, and thus the enemy of a child is the enemy of the father.
If the enemy of the child is not eliminated, the enemy of the father will likewise not be eliminated.
"To eliminate, in this manner, both old age, sickness, and death—this is what is meant by a Bodhisattva.
This is the combined analogy.
The followers of the Two Vehicles merely eliminate their own grievances, whereas the Bodhisattva possesses the way of universal salvation.
“The sick bodhisattva reflects:
‘Just as my own illness is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
This second section clarifies the gains and losses regarding self-cultivation and the taming of others through transformation.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
first, clarifying the gains and losses of self-discipline to fulfill the aforementioned practice for oneself;
second, clarifying the gains and losses of disciplining others to fulfill the aforementioned practice for others.

The third is the union with clarity regarding the gains and losses of one’s own practice and the transformation of others through subduing; this constitutes the aforementioned union with clarity for both self-practice and the transformation of others. As for the necessity of understanding these gains and losses:

when people among the world wish to act as Bodhisattvas for their own practice and the transformation of others, they look down upon the Two Vehicles and rejoice in the Great Way. However, although they study the Bodhisattva practices, there are those who are skillful and those who are unskillful; thus, gains and losses arise, and it is necessary to clarify them.
The initial passage merely distinguishes their attainment and briefly does not clarify their loss.
"As for this illness of mine, it is neither real nor existent" describes the Bodhisattva’s own realization;
"the illnesses of sentient beings are also neither real nor existent" clarifies that sentient beings have not yet attained such understanding.

The preceding discussion established that birth, old age, and death are the maladies of the body, while the conception of a self and the grasping at objects are the maladies of the mind; these two maladies are neither real nor existent.

Some say: "Non-true" means it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and "non-existent" means it is not the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); this is precisely the Middle Way and right contemplation.
Furthermore, they say that "non-true" does not mean it is not real, but rather that it is not [inherently] substantial by nature.
"Non-existence" refers to that which is neither a causal existence nor a conventional existence; thus, through the dual negation of these natures, one realizes the emptiness of the "disease.
As for understanding the emptiness of the disease: if the disease were substantially real, then the diseases of both oneself and others could not be eliminated.
Because they are not truly real, they can be eliminated.
Because they can be eliminated, compassion arises and the great vow is initiated; thus, there is the way of universal salvation.
"When performing this contemplation, if one gives rise to great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it.
This second section clarifies the gains and losses regarding the transformation of others.
If one can, as described above, give rise to compassion by realizing that the illnesses of oneself and of sentient beings are neither real nor existent, then one will only attain non-loss;
however, this contemplation has not yet been achieved.
To perceive sentient beings and give rise to compassion out of attachment is called "great compassion based on attachment and views.
Here, "perceiving" refers to the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*), and "attachment" refers to the latent tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*).
Although this involves a compassionate mind, because it is intermingled with attachment and views, it should be abandoned.
"Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions and gives rise to great compassion.
This explains the meaning of abandoning attachment and views mentioned above.

The mind is fundamentally pure and free from defilement; yet, due to the conditions of false conceptualization, attachment and views arise adventitiously. Therefore, they are called "adventitious dust," and it is to remove this adventitious dust that one gives rise to compassion.
"One who possesses attachment and views, and feels compassion [for sentient beings], will have a mind of weariness and aversion toward birth and death;
if one can distance oneself from these, there will be no weariness, and wherever one is born, one will not be obscured by attachment and views."
Now, wherever there is seeing, there must be obstruction; wherever there is love, there must be hatred. This is the way of the finite; how can it bring about the function of the infinite?

If one can be free from this, then the Dharma-body is born through transformation, being neither present nor absent; since birth and death are endless, one does not perceive them as distant. How, then, could there be the obscuration of craving and views, or the exhaustion of weariness?
"Those who are born are without bondage, yet they are able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to liberate them from their bonds.
Once attachment and views have been eliminated and the Dharma-body has been established, then those who are born are without bondage, and they are likewise able to liberate others from their bonds.
“As the Buddha has said:
‘It is impossible that one who is themselves bound could liberate another from their bonds;
it is possible that one who is themselves unbound could liberate another from their bonds.’”
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
This citation of the Buddha’s own words serves to authenticate the meaning of great compassion and exhorts the relinquishing of bondage.
"What is meant by bondage?"
"What is meant by 'liberation'?
This refers back to the Buddha’s previous statement; here, he explains bondage and liberation, which marks the headings for these two sections:
"Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva; arising through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva."
This is the section explaining bondage and liberation through the two gates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Now, first we shall proceed by way of the gate of concentration.
There are two kinds of faults in being greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*):
The first clarifies one's own practice, and the second clarifies transforming others; thus, they constitute bondage.
If one takes birth for the sake of sentient beings, then both self and others receive benefit; this is called skillful means, and is therefore termed liberation.
"Furthermore, there is bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means, and liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means;
there is bondage through skillful means lacking wisdom, and liberation through skillful means accompanied by wisdom.
This explains the meaning of bondage from the perspective of wisdom.
The preceding section sets forth two chapters:
first, clarifying the bondage and liberation of wisdom; second, indicating the bondage and liberation of skillful means.
Regarding the bondage and liberation of wisdom: because it lacks skillful means, wisdom is bound.
If there is skillful means, it is liberated through wisdom.
Skillful means is likewise so: without wisdom, skillful means becomes bondage; with wisdom, skillful means is liberation.
"What is meant by being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, yet seeks to discipline himself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is called being bound by wisdom lacking skillful means."
This explains the topical outline of the binding and liberation of wisdom; the former explains binding, and the latter explains liberation.
As for what is called "wisdom-convenience" (prajñopāya), its meaning is distinct [from mere wisdom].
Now, following the intention of Kumārajīva: observing emptiness without realizing it and traversing existence without clinging—these two skills are called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
From the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) downward, one is not yet unimpeded; when observing emptiness at those levels, one simply does not grasp or cling to anything.

When they emerge from contemplation to adorn the land and transform sentient beings, they give rise to views of attachment; thus, they are clumsy when engaging with movement, yet subtle in quiet contemplation.
Nevertheless, while contemplating emptiness without grasping at signs is indeed a skillful means, it receives its name primarily from the aspect of wisdom.
Therefore, this passage merely takes the engagement with existence without clinging to it as being called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Question:

Examining Master Kumārajīva’s interpretation, it simply explains that the meanings of wisdom (*prajñā*) and expedient means (*upāya*) are distinct; however, the reason why wisdom and expedient means constitute bondage or liberation has not yet been seen.
"Please explain this for me.
He replied:
"In the first gate, when defilement arises in accordance with what exists, it is called 'lack of skillful means' (anupāya)."
Entering emptiness to discipline oneself is called wisdom.
However, if a practitioner cannot use this wisdom of emptiness to guide their engagement with existence so that they remain unattached, then this wisdom of emptiness is termed a bondage.

Furthermore, because one cannot immediately cultivate the two practices of adorning the buddha-land and transforming sentient beings while abiding in the three emptinesses, this wisdom of emptiness is termed "bondage.
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means"?

That is to say, not adorning buddha-fields or bringing sentient beings to maturity with a mind of attachment or views, but rather disciplining oneself within the realm of the empty, signless, and wishless without weariness—this is called "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means."
This explains the section on "the liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.

Master Kumārajīva said: "From the seventh stage upward, one attains simultaneous contemplation; therefore, one is able to realize that movement and stillness are non-dual, which is termed 'liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.'"
Question:
What is meant by "liberation through wisdom"?
Answer:
Adorning the buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings according to their needs without clinging to names is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*);
entering emptiness to self-discipline is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
One who practices in this manner can lead existence by means of emptiness; because there is no attachment, the meaning of expedient means is established.
Furthermore, when one understands through wisdom, one is able to cultivate the two practices based on the three emptinesses; therefore, it is called "liberation through wisdom.
What is meant by "being bound by skillful means without wisdom"?

This means that when a bodhisattva dwells amidst afflictions such as desire, anger, and wrong views while planting the roots of all virtues, this is called "the bondage of skillful means lacking wisdom."
This explains the topical outline concerning the bondage and liberation of skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, first explaining the section on bondage:
if this refers to the bondage and liberation of wisdom (*prajñā*), its bondage and liberation are discussed in relation to the stages from the sixth ground downward and the seventh ground upward.
This first pair discusses bondage and liberation from the stage of initial resolve upward through to the noble stages.

Furthermore, regarding this first pair, it addresses bondage and liberation by contrasting the two vehicles with the bodhisattvas: the two vehicles constitute bondage, while the bodhisattvas constitute liberation.
This discussion contrasts the bondage and liberation of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) with those of bodhisattvas; ordinary beings are in bondage, while bodhisattvas are liberated.
If this is the case, then all meanings are fully encompassed without exception.
Now, first we clarify those who are bound by the absence of wisdom and skillful means: they are called "lacking wisdom" because they cannot contemplate emptiness to sever delusions;
they are said to "possess skillful means" because they engage in virtuous practices within the realm of existence.

One who practices in this manner engages with the conditioned through a lack of wisdom and is defiled by the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); therefore, it is called "the bondage of skillful means.
Furthermore, because such a person cannot traverse the three gates of liberation while remaining within these two modes of practice, it is called "the bondage of skillful means lacking wisdom."
"What is meant by liberation through the skillful means of wisdom?

It refers to planting the roots of all virtues while remaining free from afflictions such as greed, hatred, and wrong views, and then dedicating them toward unexcelled bodhi; this is called liberation through the skillful means of wisdom."
This commentary explains the section on "possessing wisdom" (*prajñā*) for the sake of understanding through wisdom.
This clarifies that contemplating emptiness to eliminate delusions is called "possessing wisdom," while engaging with existence to cultivate goodness is called "possessing skillful means" (*upāya*).
One who practices in this way, because they possess wisdom, guides their conditioned conduct without attachment;
therefore, it is called "liberation. "Mañjuśrī!
A bodhisattva who is ill should contemplate all phenomena in this manner."

From the preceding passage stating that [the body] is neither real nor existent, up to this present text, it is an exhortation for the bodhisattva to rely upon these words to initiate contemplative practice.
Furthermore, "to contemplate the body as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is called wisdom."
To clearly realize non-self is called wisdom;
though the body may be afflicted by illness, to constantly remain within the cycle of birth and death to benefit all beings without weariness is called skillful means.
In the preceding section, we have roughly clarified the two wisdoms of emptiness and existence, as well as the provisional and the real; these are also the two paths of emptiness and compassion.
Now, we shall explain wisdom and skillful means by means of the five gates of contemplation.

Since the true wisdom has been elucidated through the contemplation of the five gates, it follows that true wisdom fully illuminates both emptiness and existence. Just as illuminating impermanence and suffering constitutes the wisdom of existence, illuminating emptiness and non-self is called the wisdom of emptiness; thus, one knows that true wisdom fully illuminates both emptiness and existence.
Question:
Illuminating impermanence and suffering—how is this true wisdom?
Answer:
This body is truly impermanent; therefore, it is called "real.
Furthermore, contemplating the reality of impermanence can destroy the inversion of permanence; therefore, it is called "real.
Moreover, this text concerns the four types of impermanence in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is called "real."
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles contemplate impermanence and consequently grow weary of birth and death, desiring to enter nirvana; this is called a lack of skillful means.
The Bodhisattva contemplates impermanence yet is able to remain without weariness, thereby skillfully entering into the perilous and difficult; thus, it is called skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

"Furthermore, one contemplates the body: that the body is not separate from illness and illness is not separate from the body; that this illness and this body are neither new nor old—this is called wisdom.
That although the body may have illness, it is not eternally extinguished—this is called skillful means."
This passage specifically clarifies the two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—by means of bodily illness.
This is the diseased body; the body itself is the illness. Since there is no separate essence, how can one regard the body as the "old" and the illness as the "new"?
Once one realizes that there is neither new nor old, there is neither illness nor body; one then enters into true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*), and is thus called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Possessing this wisdom, one is able to share the same illnesses as all beings and does not grasp at *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Question:
For what reason is true wisdom explained in terms of the body and illness being inseparable, as well as the absence of newness and antiquity?
Answer:
Because those who first practice are weary of illness yet remain attached to the body.
Now, since this body and its illness cannot be separated from one another, why are you weary of the illness while still cherishing and clinging to the body?
Furthermore, he causes them to realize that the body and the illness exist only through mutual dependence; because they lack substantial reality, they are empty.
For these reasons, he makes this statement: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"A sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind.
This third section clarifies the contemplation of dual relinquishment.
This passage distantly concludes the chapter on disciplining the mind and proximately concludes the gains and losses regarding the two types of wisdom mentioned above.
One who can realize such gain and loss has tamed the mind.
They do not abide within that state, nor do they abide in an untamed mind. Why is this?
"To abide in an undisciplined mind is the way of fools;
to abide in a disciplined mind is the way of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in either a disciplined mind or an undisciplined mind."
To be free from these two dharmas is the practice of a bodhisattva.
From the preceding section upward, it has clarified *vinaya* (discipline).

Now, it clarifies that which is neither disciplined nor undisciplined. For those who are deluded, upon hearing the term "discipline," they abandon non-discipline and abide in discipline; yet their minds remain undisciplined.
If one can abandon both the disciplined and the undisciplined, such that the mind has no point of reliance and attains right contemplation, this is truly the method for disciplining the mind.
To remain within birth and death without defiling conduct, and to abide in nirvana without entering final extinction—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
It is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor the practice of noble sages; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
It is not a defiled practice, nor a pure practice; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Although it transcends the practices of Māra, it manifests the subduing of all Māras; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
"Though one seeks omniscience, there is no seeking at the improper time; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
This passage clarifies, through the sequence of dharmas, that right contemplation constitutes their discipline.

Whether both the ordinary and the sage are forgotten, or both cause and effect are transcended; whether one wanders through universal extinction, or employs one while relinquishing the other—all of these are easily understood.
There is no such thing as seeking at an improper time: when all-knowledge has not yet been accomplished, to realize the fruit of the two vehicles midway is called seeking at an improper time.
"Though one contemplates that all phenomena are unarisen, one does not enter the stage of certainty; this is the practice of a bodhisattva."
The "correct position" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) refers to the stage of attaining realization in the Hīnayāna.

While those of the three vehicles equally contemplate non-arising (*anutpāda*), those with weak power of wisdom are unable to emerge from it on their own; those with weak power of wisdom transcend it without yet attaining realization.
"Though one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, to enter into various false views—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Contemplating dependent origination is the path for severing false views; yet, to be able to intentionally conform to false views is something beyond the capacity of those of the Two Vehicles.
"Though they embrace all sentient beings, they do not harbor attachment; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
"Embracing" refers to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The four methods of attraction are the means by which one cherishes and cares for sentient beings; here, it is clarified that while there is affection, there is no attachment.
"Though one delights in seclusion, not relying on the exhaustion of body and mind—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Minor seclusion is the departure from clamor and bustle; great seclusion is the departure from the exhaustion of body and mind. Although the bodhisattva delights in great seclusion, they do not rely upon it.
"Though they traverse the three realms, they do not destroy the dharma-nature; this is the bodhisattva practice.
Since the three realms are themselves the dharma-nature, they manifest within the three realms without destroying the dharma-nature.
"Though practicing emptiness, one plants the roots of all virtues; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To practice emptiness with the intent to eliminate existence, yet simultaneously plant the roots of all virtues, is precisely for emptiness to possess utility.
"Though practicing signlessness, yet delivering sentient beings—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To practice signlessness while desiring to eliminate the grasping at the signs of sentient beings, and thereby deliver them, is by means of the signless and unimpeded sign.
"Though practicing non-action, manifesting the reception of a body—this is the bodhisattva practice.
To practice non-action while desiring not to create birth and death, yet through skillful means manifesting the reception of a body, means that non-action does not obstruct action.
"Though practicing non-arising, yet giving rise to all wholesome practices—this is the bodhisattva practice.

"Non-arising" means that in all circumstances, the mind ultimately does not arise; yet one simultaneously gives rise to all wholesome practices, because through non-arising there is nothing that does not arise.
"Though practicing the six pāramitās, to thoroughly know the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings is the bodhisattva practice.

Although the six perfections are all phenomena without marks (*animitta*), and that which is without marks should have nothing to be known, one nonetheless thoroughly knows the mental activities of sentient beings; this is because through non-knowing, there is nothing that is not known.
"Though one practices the six supernormal powers, not exhausting the outflows—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Because the Great Being perceives that outflows are themselves non-outflows, he is able to dwell eternally within birth and death and share the same outflows as all beings; how could he differ from those who have exhausted their outflows by means of such exhaustion?
"Though one practices the four immeasurable minds, not being greedily attached to rebirth in the Brahma world—this is the bodhisattva practice.

Although the practice of the four immeasurables should lead to birth in the stages of the four dhyānas, the text specifically mentions the Brahma world because sentient beings take the Brahma Heaven as their primary object of veneration; thus, it cites that which they revere.
Furthermore, the stages of the four dhyānas are collectively termed "Brahma.
"Though one practices meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi, yet does not take birth according to those dhyānas—this is the practice of a bodhisattva."
"Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas.
"Samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti).
"Vimokṣa" refers to the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa).
The samādhis are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
When a bodhisattva practices their causes but does not grasp at their fruits, this may be called "sovereign practice."
"Although one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, never ultimately becoming separated from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena— this is the bodhisattva practice.
While those of the Lesser Vehicle contemplate these four dharmas and thereby attain realization,
the bodhisattva, though contemplating these same four dharmas, does not attain realization by means of ultimate separation from them.
"Though practicing the four right efforts, not abandoning physical and mental diligence—this is the bodhisattva practice.
While those of the Lesser Vehicle practice the four right efforts and, upon the completion of their application, abandon them by entering nirvana;
the bodhisattva, though performing the same practices, does not share in that abandonment.
"Though practicing the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), one attains sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); this is the bodhisattva practice.
Although they practice the bases of psychic power similarly to those of the Hīnayāna, they have long since attained the sovereign supernormal powers of the Mahāyāna.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are the cause of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"Though one practices the five faculties (*indriya*), yet discerns whether the faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull—this is the bodhisattva practice."
Those of the Lesser Vehicle cultivate only their own faculties and are not skilled at knowing the faculties of others;
although Bodhisattvas likewise cultivate themselves, they are skilled at knowing the faculties of others.
"Though they practice the five powers, they joyfully seek the ten powers of a Buddha—this is the conduct of a Bodhisattva."
"Though one practices the seven factors of enlightenment, yet discerns the wisdom of a Buddha—this is the bodhisattva practice.
Though one practices the eightfold noble path, yet delights in practicing the immeasurable path of the Buddhas—this is the bodhisattva practice."
This clarifies that while manifesting shallow dharmas, one has in fact already entered deeply into profound dharmas.
"Though practicing the dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā that assist the path, not ultimately falling into quiescent extinction—this is the bodhisattva practice."

Regarding the distinction between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) on one hand, and *samādhi* (concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom) on the other: concentration and wisdom are the fruit, while calm abiding and insight are the cause.
Initially fixing the mind upon an object is called calm abiding;
profoundly penetrating through discernment is termed insight.
These two are dharmas that assist toward nirvāṇa.
The bodhisattva practices because of them, yet does not need to follow after nirvāṇa.
Although he practices all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, he adorns his body with the primary and secondary marks; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas while not abandoning the Buddha-dharma is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To accord with the ultimately pure characteristics of all phenomena while manifesting bodies according to what is appropriate for beings is the practice of a bodhisattva.
"Though one contemplates that all Buddha-lands are eternally quiescent like space, yet manifests various kinds of pure Buddha-lands—this is the bodhisattva practice.
Though one attains the Buddha-way, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, yet does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva—this is the bodhisattva practice."
Although the attainment of the Buddha-way is ultimately empty, one manifests the practice of causes; thus, the fruit does not obstruct the cause.
"When this Dharma was being taught, among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī, eight thousand devaputras all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This is the third question concerning matters following an illness.
The various editions of the sutra differ, with some referring to the "deva assembly" (天眾) and others to the "great assembly" (大眾); there is no contradiction in this.
Nevertheless, it should indeed be the "great assembly."
Chapter Six: The Inconceivable (4). This sixth chapter, "The Inconceivable," which uses great illumination to transform sentient beings, has two gates:
first, the preaching of the Dharma; second, the manifestation of supernatural powers.

The first chapter, "Inquiring after Illness," clarifies his preaching of the Dharma; now this current chapter further clarifies his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which benefit sentient beings through both form and voice.

Furthermore, in the preceding chapter, it first clarifies the illness of the one who transforms—consisting of the two paths of emptiness and compassion, which are likewise the provisional and the real, and wisdom;
next, it clarifies the illness of those who are transformed, which likewise consists of the two paths of emptiness and compassion, and the two types of wisdom: the provisional and the real.
The explanation of these two types of wisdom—the wisdom of the transformer and the wisdom of the transformed—is intended to instruct bodhisattvas on the meaning of practice.
Now, this chapter clarifies that when practice reaches fulfillment, there arises boundless and great function; therefore, there follows the "Chapter on the Inconceivable."
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the inconceivable?
Answer:
To discuss these matters comprehensively, there are three principles:
first, the inconceivable realm; second, inconceivable wisdom; and third, inconceivable teaching.

Speaking in terms of the capacity for transformation, wisdom is generated from the realm, and the teaching is expounded on account of wisdom. This is intended so that those who are to be transformed may, by means of the teaching, awaken to the principle, and through the principle, generate wisdom. Therefore, within these three gates, there is nothing of the meaning that is not subsumed.
Regarding what is called the "inconceivable realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*), it is precisely the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional; yet these two truths have never been a [static] object.
When the teaching is based on the manifestation of principle, the two truths are termed "teaching" (*śāsana*);
when considered from the perspective of the arising of wisdom, the two truths are named "realm."

Speaking generally, both these realms of the ultimate and the conventional are, by their very nature, dependently originated, provisionally designated, and devoid of anything to be apprehended; they cannot be conceived by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles who perceive things as having substantial existence. Therefore, these two realms are termed "inconceivable."

According to a separate treatise, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, the mind cannot conceive of it; because speech is also cut off, the mouth cannot discuss it. Thus, the ultimate truth is called "inconceivable."

The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is likewise beyond the path of language and where the movements of the mind cease. Since it is a provisional existence that cannot be definitively said to exist, the mind that seeks to fixate on its existence ceases;
since it is a provisional existence that cannot be definitively said to be non-existent, the mind that seeks to fixate on its non-existence ceases;

since it cannot be definitively said to be both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent, the mind that seeks to fixate on these four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*) ceases. Furthermore, because it is of a nature that cannot be expressed through the four positions, this conventional truth is inconceivable.

Next, to clarify the inconceivability of the two wisdoms: true wisdom is precisely *prajñā*. Since *prajñā* transcends conceptualization, observation, and delusion, and even linguistic expression is severed, the mind cannot conceive of it and the mouth cannot discuss it.

Skillful means and wisdom are changeable and without fixed form, like a large vessel containing smaller ones; they cannot be conceived by ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas of the lower stages, and are thus called "inconceivable."

Regarding what is called the inconceivability of the teaching: internally, there are two wisdoms which constitute the inconceivable source; externally, the manifestation of form and sound constitutes the inconceivable trace. This means that the source is manifested through the trace.
Through the inconceivable traces on the outside, one attains the revelation of the inconceivable source; that is to say, the source is manifested by means of the traces.
This is fully explained as set forth in the "Mysterious Chapter" (Xuánzhāng).
Within this present chapter, two major sections are extensively opened:
First, the inconceivability of the wisdom of reality; second, the inconceivability of the wisdom of skillful means.

The first section contains five parts: 1. Śāriputra’s thought regarding the seat; 2. Vimalakīrti’s reprimand and interrogation; 3. Śāriputra’s response; 4. Vimalakīrti’s further reprimand; 5. The assembly’s realization of the Way.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, had this thought:
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and the assembly of great disciples sit?"
The Venerable Śāriputra gave rise to this thought based on two meanings:
first, speaking according to outward manifestation.

While the Great Beings of the Dharma-body experience neither physical nor mental fatigue, the śrāvaka’s form is shaped by the karma of fetters; though his mind is free of fetters, his body undergoes exhaustion, and thus he manifests the appearance of seeking rest.
Because he was among the disciples the most senior in years and physically frail, he recalled his former lives; moreover, he did not wish to manifest his past failings.
Furthermore, he surely knew that Vimalakīrti had already scrutinized his mind from afar, and thus he merely thought it in his heart without speaking a word.
Secondly, speaking from the perspective of their fundamental capacities:

since Vimalakīrti and Śāriputra were both individuals of the Great and Small Vehicles respectively, they each transformed sentient beings in their own way; thus, Vimalakīrti prepared an empty room to receive his guest, while Śāriputra contemplated his seating arrangement before delivering his teaching.
The elder Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think,
worthy one?"
"Have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or do you seek a seat?
This was Vimalakīrti’s way of elucidating the path of non-seeking; thus, he questioned him.
The reason for this is that the thought of needing to sit leaves traces of seeking, and where there is seeking, one deviates from the Principle (Li); such is not the true intent of his coming.
Śāriputra said:
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a seat.
By thus affirming two realities, Śāriputra fell into defeat through his own vacillation.
If it were the Dharma, one should not think of sitting;
if one thinks of sitting, how can that be called the Dharma?
Yet Śāriputra answered one question exclusively; he came originally for the sake of the Dharma, but because his body was weary, he sought a seat.
Furthermore, when the body is at ease, the Dharma enters the spirit; thus, even the thought of sitting [in meditation] ultimately becomes the Dharma.
Vimalakīrti said: "O Śāriputra!..."
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not cling to body or life, much less to beds and seats.

One who seeks the Dharma does not seek by way of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor do they seek by way of the elements (dhātus) or the sense bases (āyatanas); nor do they seek by way of the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
O Śāriputra! One who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the Saṅgha.
One who seeks the Dharma has no seeking that views suffering, no seeking that abandons the origin [of suffering], no seeking that realizes cessation, and no seeking that cultivates the path.
Why is this so? Because phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path," this is conceptual proliferation; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
"O Śāriputra! The Dharma is named 'quiescence.
If one practices with arising and ceasing, one is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named 'stainless. If one becomes defiled by the Dharma, even up to Nirvāṇa, this is attachment; it is not seeking the Dharma."
The Dharma has no place for practice; if one practices within the Dharma, that is a place of practice and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma is without grasping or abandoning; if one grasps or abandons the Dharma, that is grasping and abandoning and not the seeking of the Dharma.
The Dharma has no location; if one clings to a location, that is clinging to a place, not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma is named "signlessness" (animitta); if one follows signs with consciousness, that is seeking signs, not seeking the Dharma.
"The Dharma cannot be dwelt upon; if one dwells in the Dharma, that is dwelling in the Dharma and not seeking the Dharma.
The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known; if one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, that is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and not seeking the Dharma."
These six faculties are subsumed into four functions: the eye for seeing, the ear for hearing, the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body for sensing, and the faculty of mind for cognizing.
“The Dharma is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). If one practices the conditioned, one is seeking the conditioned and not seeking the Dharma.
Therefore, Śāriputra, if one seeks the Dharma, one should seek nothing at all among all dharmas.”
This chapter elucidates non-seeking, and its purport is twofold:

first, it reveals the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), which transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; the path of language is severed and the movements of the mind are extinguished. One cannot seek the true mark through categories such as existence or non-existence; this explains the inconceivable realm.
Second, it is intended to cause the practitioner to accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*) and to also cease all states of mind that grasp at existence.

The reason for this is that when the mind has something to seek, there is attachment; when there is attachment, there is bondage, and thus one cannot achieve liberation. How much more so if one deviates from the true nature? Therefore, the mind is made to have nothing to seek.
Because the mind has nothing to seek, the activities of the mind are severed and speech is extinguished;

this is precisely inconceivable true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). Since the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be sought, there is no numerical reckoning externally; since true wisdom has nothing to seek, there is no mind internally. Thus, object and wisdom are simultaneously merged in darkness, and conditions and contemplation are both stilled; this is the ultimate principle, truly inconceivable.
"When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Because they realized that both the object of perception and the perceiving subject are quiescent, and that both the internal and external are simultaneously darkened [in stillness], all acquired defilements and burdens were stilled; thus it is called the "pure Dharma-eye."
However, the purification of the Dharma-eye has two meanings:
according to the Hīnayāna, it refers to the fruit of Srotāpanna;
with respect to the Mahāyāna, it refers to a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*), because in the Mahāyāna, the first stage is considered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Master Sengzhao said: "This text is the purification of the Mahāyāna Dharma-eye.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī:

"Virtuous One, you travel through immeasurable, thousands-of-myriads-of-asamkhyeya lands; in which Buddha-field are there lion thrones so well adorned with the accomplishment of supreme and wondrous merits?"
This second section further clarifies the inconceivable nature of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Having previously demonstrated that there is nothing to be sought, one thereby accords with the true reality (*dharmatā*); thus, one is able to universally provide for all that sentient beings seek.
Within the text, this is broadly divided into two sections:
first, a brief exposition on the inconceivability of the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); second, a detailed explanation of the inconceivability of the provisional wisdom.
The initial section consists of ten phrases:

1. Vimalakīrti’s inquiry; 2. Mañjuśrī’s response; 3. Vimalakīrti borrows a seat; 4. King Dīpaṃkara sends a seat; 5. The great assembly offers praise; 6. Vimalakīrti commands the bodhisattvas to take their seats; 7. The bodhisattvas accept the instruction and sit; 8. Vimalakīrti instructs the śrāvakas to take their seats; 9. Śāriputra and the others are unable to do so; 10. He again instructs them to pay homage to King Dīpaṃkara.
This is the first point.

As for why Vimalakīrti asked this question: first, he wished to have the guest himself choose the most excellent host; thus, there ought to be a matter of taking and giving, and for this reason he questioned him.
Second, he wished to inspire a sense of reverence and faith in the assembly.
Had he taken [the seat] without asking, it might have been suspected as something created by illusion;
now that he takes it only after being asked, they know for certain that a real seat has arrived.
There are two reasons for borrowing a seat from another region:
first, to manifest the extraordinary excellence of the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruits of maturation) upon which the merits of all Buddhas rely, thereby inspiring the assembly to aspire toward Buddhahood;
second, to utilize the matter of the journey to cause the transformative influence of both nations to flow forth.
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder!
To the east, beyond thirty-six Ganges-sands of worlds, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa; its Buddha is named Sumeru-pradīpa-rāja, and he currently dwells there."
That Buddha’s body is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height, and his lion throne is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, being the most exquisitely adorned of all.
This was the second answer given by Mañjuśrī.
Master Zhao said: "The *yojana*, a measure of distance in India, is not fixed; the superior *yojana* is sixty *li*, the middling *yojana* is fifty *li*, and the inferior *yojana* is forty *li*."
"Then the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernatural powers.
This is the third instance of Vimalakīrti borrowing seats;
because those bodhisattvas were to come from the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation," he dispatched a transformation-body to remain there.
In the land of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there are no assemblies of beings; therefore, he merely manifests supernatural powers through silence.

Furthermore, these two chapters mutually clarify what is extraordinary: this chapter distinguishes how the large enters the small, while that chapter clarifies how the small accommodates the large. Thus, that chapter explains the dispatching of emanations, whereas this chapter demonstrates the silent response.
"Immediately, that Buddha dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, vast, majestic, and pure—which entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
This is the fourth instance of King Lamp dispatching thrones.
Although Vimalakīrti had gone to fetch it by means of his supernatural powers, that Buddha did not send it, and thus there was no way for it to arrive.

The bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings—all of whom had never before seen it—beheld his room as vast and expansive, fully accommodating thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction. Furthermore, neither the city of Vaiśālī nor the four continents of Jambudvīpa were compressed or crowded; everything appeared exactly as it had been before.
The assembly of the fifth period praised this.
Question:
To enter the great into the small, without the small increasing or the great decreasing, is inconceivable.
Now, since it is said that the chamber is vast and expansive, this would imply an increase in its size; how then can it be called "unfathomable"?
Answer:
When viewed from within, the chamber appears vast and expansive, yet when viewed from without, its original appearance remains as it was; thus, there is no actual increase.
Question:
When viewed from the outside, the fundamental appearance remains as it was, so one need not increase what is external;
but when viewed from within, the chamber appears vast and expansive—should one then increase what is internal?
Answer:
The Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) truly is able not to increase [the space] within; he merely wishes to manifest two kinds of inconceivability:
first, sitting in his great seat while entering a small room, yet the external appearance of the small room remains as it was—this is the inconceivability of the large and the small.

Second, to clarify the inconceivability of its interior and exterior: there is but a single chamber of one *fangzhang* (ten feet square). Viewed from within, it appears vast; viewed from without, it remains precisely that same ten-foot square. Thus, it is the inconceivability of both interior and exterior.
Another interpretation is as follows:

it is not large within because people see that the room accommodates the seats; thus, it is said that the small room has been altered, and therefore it is stated next that its original characteristics remain as they were.
The original characteristics remain as they were; ultimately, the external appearance does not diminish, nor does the internal increase.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, "Please take a seat upon this lion throne."
"Sitting together with the various bodhisattvas and superior persons, you should manifest yourself as being like those seated figures.
This sixth section clarifies the instruction for the bodhisattvas to take their seats.
"The bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers immediately transformed their bodies to be forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height and sat upon lion thrones."
"None of the newly resolved bodhisattvas or the great disciples were able to ascend.
For the seventh time, he received the instruction and sat down.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:
"Ascend the lion throne.
This was the eighth instruction given to the śrāvakas. Śāriputra said:
"Layman! This seat is high and wide; I cannot ascend it.
Thus, the ninth śrāvaka was unable to take his place on the seat.
There are two meanings to this:

first, it was constrained by the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti, who wished to cause sentient beings to know that the superiority and inferiority of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are as vastly different as this.
Second, it is the seat of the merits of all Buddhas; it is not a seat for those without merit. Its principle is inherently profound and transcendent, beyond being subject to constraint.
Vimalakīrti said: "O Śāriputra!..."
"If you pay homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja, you will then be able to sit.
This is the tenth exhortation to pay homage to Dīparāja.
Since he is Dīparāja, by performing prostrations to him, one receives the Buddha’s spiritual power and thus gains the ability to sit.

Thereupon, the bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds and the great disciples prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja and immediately gained the ability to sit upon the lion throne.
Śāriputra said:
"Householder!

It is truly unprecedented that such a small room can accommodate these high and vast seats, yet without obstructing the city of Vaiśālī, nor crowding the palaces of the devas, nāgas, rājās, ghosts, and spirits throughout the villages, cities, and towns of Jambudvīpa, or across the four continents."
Below this is the second section, the detailed explanation of the inconceivable.
It consists of five parts according to the text:

first, Śāriputra takes his seat and offers praise; second, Vimalakīrti provides a pure explanation; third, Kāśyapa alternates between suppression and exaltation; fourth, the assembly receives benefit; and fifth, Vimalakīrti again praises the inconceivable.
Vimalakīrti said: "O Śāriputra!
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess a liberation called 'Inconceivable'."
The second section is the explanation of the "Pure Name.
As for the essence of liberation, it refers to the wisdom of the provisional and the real.

It is, in fact, a single correct contemplation; however, for the sake of sentient beings, it is described through various names: sometimes it is called "liberation," sometimes it is termed "nirvana," sometimes it receives the title of "prajñā," and again it is established under the designation of the "One Vehicle."
Now, when we speak of liberation (vimukti), there are generally two meanings:
first, its essence is unimpeded; second, its function is sovereign.
As for sovereignty: if one desires to act but is unable to do so, that is bondage.
Because one can act as soon as one intends, and there is nothing that cannot be liberated from, it is called "liberation.

A Great Being (Mahāsattva) is capable of this; however, ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas of lower stages do not know what it is that can be so accomplished. Therefore, it is called "inconceivable" (acintya).
This is the name of the liberation that emerges.

"If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, he can place the height and breadth of Mount Sumeru inside a mustard seed without any increase or decrease; the original appearance of the King of Mountains, Sumeru, remains as it was. Yet the Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven do not perceive or know where they have entered. Only those who are ready for deliverance see Mount Sumeru enter into the mustard seed. This is called the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation."
From this point onward, the thirteen subsequent sections explain the function of liberation; that is, they manifest the fundamental through its traces.
These thirteen sections are divided into three parts:
the first eleven matters clarify the inconceivable by way of external dharmas that are the fruits of reliance.
The next single point clarifies the inconceivable by means of internal form;
the thirteenth single point clarifies the inconceivable by means of sound.
Regarding the first clarification—that the Great enters the Small without increase or decrease—some say:
A large substantial entity does not actually enter a small one; rather, it is through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that beings perceive it as entering.
Some say: because a large substantial entity can contain a small one, it causes beings to perceive it so.
Now it is said that there are two meanings:
first, although in reality they do not enter, they enable one to see them as entering;
second, in reality they enable one to enter, being appropriately suited to the conditions.
Question:
Since the small and the large neither increase nor decrease, how can they be contained within one another?
Answer:
Some say: Since it is described as "inconceivable," one merely exalts the realm of the sages and has no means to explain it. Others say:
The large lacks the characteristics of largeness, therefore the large can enter the small;
the small lacks the characteristics of smallness, therefore the small can contain the large.
Now, it is said that both of these two explanations are incorrect.
If there were no characteristics of smallness or greatness, what could be contained within?
If smallness and greatness possessed fixed natures, then that which is not contained would likewise possess a fixed nature.
That which is fixedly uncontainable cannot be made to appear as contained; therefore, even smallness and greatness with fixed natures have no mutual containment.
Now, as for the statement that they "can contain one another," it is because they can contain one another through the provisional designation of causes and conditions.
That which is large is called "large" in relation to the small, and thus the large can enter the small;
that which is small is "small" in relation to the large, and thus the small can contain the large.
Question:
If the small does not increase, how can it accommodate the large?
Answer:

It is like a mirror an inch wide hanging on a wall that reflects the entire world; all things in the world appear exhaustively within the mirror, yet the objects do not diminish and the mirror does not increase.

"Furthermore, he may cause the waters of the four great oceans to enter into a single pore without disturbing fish, turtles, crocodiles, sea-monsters, or any other aquatic creatures; yet the original appearance of that great ocean remains as it was before. The dragons, spirits, and asuras therein do not perceive or know where they have entered, nor is there any disturbance to these beings."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in this inconceivable liberation can seize the trichiliocosm like a potter’s wheel and place it in his right palm; he then hurls it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet the sentient beings therein have no awareness or knowledge of where they have gone.
Furthermore, he restores them all to their original places, such that no one perceives any coming or going, yet this world remains exactly as it was before.
Moreover, Śāriputra!

If there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and can be liberated, the Bodhisattva then expands seven days into one kalpa, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as one kalpa;

if there are sentient beings who do not delight in dwelling long and can be liberated, the Bodhisattva then contracts one kalpa into seven days, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as seven days.
From the beginning until now, the self-sovereignty of the dharma-body has been explained as the inconceivable.
This single matter is explained as the inconceivable in terms of the duration and brevity of time.
Question:

Previously, when examining the substance of dharmas to determine whether they can contain one another without increase or decrease, it was established that there is no such change. Now, in clarifying the length of time, how can there be extension or contraction?
Answer:
The inconceivable has many aspects; it cannot be categorized as a single type.
Previously, it was the inconceivable [nature] of neither increasing nor decreasing; now, it is the inconceivable [nature] clarified through both increasing and decreasing.
Question:
It may be that neither increasing nor decreasing is inconceivable.
Since there is such increase and decrease, how can it be called "unfathomable"?
Answer:

Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles at lower stages cannot shorten one kalpa to seven days, nor extend seven days to one kalpa; the Great Beings (bodhisattvas) can do so, and therefore this is inconceivable.

Furthermore, although a single kalpa may be compressed into seven days, the kalpa remains exactly as it was; and although seven days may be extended into a kalpa, the seven days remain as they were. This is why it is called "inconceivable."
Question:
How is it so? Answer:
It is like a person who, in a single night's dream, experiences a hundred years of pleasure; yet the night is not long, nor are those hundred seasons short.
Such is the conduct of the Mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation gathers the adornments of all buddha-fields into a single land and manifests them to sentient beings."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva takes the sentient beings of a single buddha-field, places them upon his right palm, and flies to the ten directions to display them everywhere, yet without moving them from their original location.
Śāriputra! Whatever offerings sentient beings of the ten directions present to the Buddhas, the bodhisattva causes them all to be seen within a single pore.
Furthermore, all the suns, moons, and stars existing in the lands of the ten directions, he causes them all to be seen universally within a single pore.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

all the great winds that exist throughout the worlds of the ten directions, a bodhisattva is able to inhale and draw into his mouth, yet his body suffers no injury, nor are the trees outside broken or shattered.

Furthermore, when the kalpas of the worlds in the ten directions are consumed by fire, he can place all those fires within his own belly; the fires continue their functions as before, yet they do no harm.

Moreover, from below, he can take a single buddha-field from among the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and lift it up to a region above as many countless worlds as there are sands in the Ganges, just as one might pick up a jujube leaf with the point of a needle without causing it any disturbance.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha, or manifest the body of a pratyekabuddha, or manifest the body of a śrāvaka, or manifest the body of Śakra, or manifest the body of Brahmā, or manifest the body of a world-protector, or manifest the body of a wheel-turning monarch.

Furthermore, all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether superior, middling, or inferior—they are all able to transform into the voice of the Buddha, producing the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, so that all may hear them universally therein.
"Śāriputra!
I have now briefly explained the power of the inconceivable liberation of a bodhisattva; were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Question:
Question: Non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles are also able to manifest in various forms and transform into diverse sounds; how do they differ from the Great Beings (Bodhisattvas)?
Answer:
Ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle cannot universally respond to all forms or universally transform into all sounds; therefore, they differ from the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the Great Being can cause his voice to reach the Summit of Existence (bhavāgra) such that no sound is heard, and his form to pervade the ten directions such that no image is seen.
Ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles cannot do so; therefore, it is called inconceivable.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard this exposition of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation dharma-gate, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to Śāriputra:
"It is as if someone were to display a multitude of forms and images before a blind person; they would not be seen by him."
It is precisely like this: when all the śrāvakas hear this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, they are unable to understand it.
When the wise hear this, who would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
"What have we done to permanently sever our roots, such that regarding this Mahāyāna, we are like withered seeds?
This was the third praise by Kāśyapa.
By extolling the Great Way and disparaging the Hīnayāna, it causes Bodhisattvas not to retreat from their superior resolve and causes Śrāvakas to feel deep self-reproach and shame.
Furthermore, it causes those who have not yet resolved upon the Great Mind to do so because of this, and enables those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle to change their aspirations by means of this.
Question:
It was stated previously that "the Great enters into the Small," and only those who are to be saved can perceive this.

Since Śāriputra is like a blind man facing an image, how could he see the great seat enter the small room? Answer: There are three types of sentient beings with great intelligence: [the one who sees the small within the large, the one who sees the large within the small, and the one who sees both simultaneously]. Śāriputra belongs to the first category. Therefore, although he saw the small room, he did not see the great seat enter it. Furthermore, there are two kinds of "smallness": first, smallness of the physical vessel; second, smallness of the mind. Śāriputra’s mind was small, whereas the Buddha’s mind was vast. Because his mind was small, he could not perceive the vastness of the Buddha’s mind. It is like a person whose eyes are covered by a cloth: even if they are shown a great palace, they can only see what is small. This is because their eyes are obstructed. It is also like a person who has never seen a great palace before: even if they are led into one, they will only perceive its small features. This is because their prior experience is limited. Śāriputra was likewise like this. His mind was narrow and his wisdom was shallow; therefore, he could not perceive the vastness of the Buddha’s mind. For these reasons, he could not see the great seat enter the small room. Furthermore, there are three types of sentient beings with great intelligence: first, those who see the small within the large; second, those who see the large within the small; third, those who see both the large and the small simultaneously. First, there are those who do not see the large enter the small, nor do they comprehend the manner by which it occurs; these are the class of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are incapable of seeing or hearing this.
Second, there are those who, though they see the large enter the small, are unable to understand it; these are the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*).
Third, seeing the large enter the small and further being able to awaken to this—such a bodhisattva is one of superior faculties.
What was stated previously—that only those who are destined for deliverance can see it—refers to persons of superior faculties.
Śāriputra, seeing this yet remaining in profound ignorance, was likened to one who is blind.
"When all śrāvakas hear this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, they should all weep aloud, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm;
all bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crown of their heads."
Because the loss suffered was so grievous, one might figuratively say they ought to weep;
yet for those of the Two Vehicles, sorrow and grief are eternally eliminated, such that they do not even shed a single tear, let alone cause the three thousandfold world-system to tremble.

Kāśyapa, intending to clarify the distinction between the Great and the Small Vehicles and to modulate his discourse according to the audience, has shown that those who do not belong to this [Great Vehicle] should weep with the longing for its gifts, while those who already belong to it should respond with the praise of receiving it upon their heads.
"If there are bodhisattvas who believe in and understand this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, all the hosts of Māra can do nothing against them.
If one can merely believe and understand it, even Māra cannot disturb them; how much more so for those who practice in accordance with it!
"When Mahākāśyapa spoke these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This was the fourth assembly's generation of the resolve.
Since Kāśyapa was himself a śrāvaka, it was logically inevitable that he would personally disparage the Small Vehicle as inferior and extol the Great Vehicle as supreme;
thus, when the devas heard this, they conceived the aspiration for Buddhahood.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa:
"O Virtuous One!

Those who act as Māras in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the liberation of the inconceivable, who, through the power of skillful means, manifest as Māras to teach and transform sentient beings."
Regarding this fifth section on the Pure Name’s reiteration of the inconceivable:
the thirteen preceding points merely described the functional application of the inconceivable in accordance with worldly norms;
they did not clarify its contrarian application. Thus, as the meaning remained incomplete, this section follows Kāśyapa’s praise to further describe that contrarian application.

Furthermore, because Kāśyapa said that those with inconceivable faith and understanding cannot be disturbed by Māra, yet there are also bodhisattvas in the ten directions who are disturbed by Māra, [the Buddha] sought to clarify that the deeds of inconceivable Mahāsattvas are sovereign; desiring to transform beginners, he manifests as a Māra-king, which is not something that the power of Māra can achieve.
This clarifies the inconceivable, fulfilling Kāśyapa’s intention: "Furthermore, Kāśyapa,

suppose there are immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions, and someone comes to them begging for their hands, feet, ears, noses, head, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, flesh, skin, bones, villages, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, conch shells, clothing, or food and drink."
"Such beggars are mostly bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who go to test them by means of skillful power, in order to make their resolve firm."
This briefly clarifies the Mahāsattva’s contrarian applications, which are of two kinds:
first, manifesting as a celestial Māra; second, appearing as a beggar. Other realms of existence may be understood by analogy.

The reason he previously acted as a beggar was that this Bodhisattva in his karmic formation had not yet reached the ultimate limit in the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). Therefore, the inconceivable Bodhisattva forcibly sought from him, so as to cause him to have no mind of stinginess and to bring his steadfastness to full completion; furthermore, it was to let sentient beings know of his steadfastness and to enable him himself to realize his own steadfastness.
Question:
Since the inconceivable Great Being perceives the faculties of others from afar, why does he resort to testing them through pressure?
Answer:
To now beg and entreat is to follow the traces of Māra’s trials; thus, it is spoken of as "testing.
It is also to advance only after waiting for the trial. Why is this so?
Because Bodhisattvas who dwell in the inconceivable liberation possess the power of majestic virtue, they exercise compulsion to demonstrate such difficult matters to all sentient beings.
Ordinary people of inferior capacity lack such power and influence; they cannot thus compel these Bodhisattvas.
"It is like a dragon-elephant treading with its feet; it is not something a donkey can do.
This explains the Bodhisattva’s capacity for rigorous testing.
To sever a person's hands and feet, to separate them from their wife and children, and to forcibly seize their national wealth—these things give rise to sorrow and grief.
Although there is slight suffering before one's eyes, it brings about great peace for eternal kalpas.
Next, the analogy of the donkey and the elephant is raised to illustrate the two meanings of "capability" and "incapability."
The most excellent among elephants is called a "nāga-elephant" (lung-hsiang), for these are not two separate things.
This is what is meant by "the gate of wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva abiding in the inconceivable liberation."

Regarding the inconceivable essence: although it comprises both object and wisdom as well as the teaching, its actual substance consists of the two types of wisdom; therefore, they are summarized here.

Wisdom is the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), and skillful means (*upāya*) is the provisional wisdom (*prajñapti-jñāna*); because these two are without [inherent] reality, they are called "gates."
Furthermore, because it compels one to awaken and enter [into reality], it is also called a "gate" (*mukha*).

Moreover, although the ultimate truth and the provisional truth have never truly existed as two, they are forcibly designated as such for the sake of sentient beings; since this [designation] enables one to penetrate the non-dual, it is called a "gate."

Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings (5).
Regarding the general meaning of the *Dafangdeng jing* (Mahāvaipulya Sūtra), there are two gates:
first, the transformer; second, those who are transformed.

The "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (Acintya-parivarta) elucidates the gate of the transformative teaching, while the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" (Satvaparīkṣā-parivarta) subsequently clarifies those who are to be transformed.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" primarily elucidates analytical wisdom (prajñā), and thus possesses boundless and wondrous functions;
the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" primarily elucidates fundamental wisdom (jñāna), meaning that sentient beings are ultimately empty.
The two wisdoms constitute the primary theme of this sutra; therefore, they are extensively discussed throughout its various chapters.

Furthermore, the preceding "Inquiry into Ailments" chapter states, "From delusion and craving, my illness arises. This clarifies the fundamental principle of the relationship between the transformer (the Buddha) and the transformed (sentient beings).

If one does not recognize sentient beings, one does not recognize the illnesses of sentient beings; if one does not recognize the illnesses of sentient beings, one has not yet attained an understanding of the illness of the bodhisattva. Therefore, it is necessary to properly recognize sentient beings, thereby fully comprehending these two meanings; this explains the purport of the preceding chapter on "The Illness."
As for what is called "observing sentient beings," "observing" refers to the term for penetrating [reality], while "sentient beings" is a designation.
The phenomena of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are called a "multitude" (gaṇa); because they assemble to form a person, they are called "beings" (sattva).
Furthermore, those who are born in a multitude of places are called *sattva* (sentient beings).
Regarding the explanation of *sattva*, there is a distinction between internal and external views.
As for the external paths, they assert that sentient beings truly exist, and there are four such theories.
The Sāṃkhya says:
"Sentient beings and the aggregates are one.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
"Sentient beings are different from the aggregates. Ṛṣabha said:
"Sentient beings are both identical to and different from the aggregates."
The son of Vatsa said:
"Sentient beings and the aggregates (skandhas) are neither identical nor different.
Within the study of the Buddha-dharma, there are generally three masters.
The Vātsīputrīyas say:
"Sentient beings truly exist.
The Sarvāstivādins clarify that there are no sentient beings.
What Harivarman establishes exists according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) but does not exist according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* employ Harivarman’s principles, and subsequently there are three explanations:
for instance, as Master Tan of Zhaoti Monastery and others clarify, sentient beings possess substance, function, and designation.
As Kaishan Zhizang said: "Sentient beings have no substance; they possess only names and functions.
Master Guangzhai Fayun said: "There is neither substance nor function; there is only a provisional name."

Now, this chapter, "Observing Sentient Beings," follows this same principle: it is both identical to the Vātsīputrīya position that [the person] substantially exists, yet distinct from the Sarvāstivāda view that [it] is entirely non-existent. As explained in detail in the text, the chapter is thus named after this subject.
This chapter is divided into two sections:
first, Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī discuss sentient beings; second, the heavenly maiden and Śāriputra successively discuss sentient beings.
The initial section contains two parts:
First, the practice of transforming others is clarified; next, the practice for oneself is clarified.
Within the practice of transforming others, there is first the contemplation of sentient beings, followed by the clarification of the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
Regarding the initial passage:
First the question, then the answer:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti,
'How should a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?'"
The reason Mañjuśrī asks this question is that the aforementioned inconceivable and boundless wondrous function is, in essence, the Dharma for transforming sentient beings.

Listeners might think there are actual sentient beings who can be transformed; therefore, it is now clarified that if sentient beings truly existed, then inconceivable matters would not be possible, and sentient beings could not be transformed.
Now, wishing to establish the relationship between the transformer and the transformed, he asks about observing sentient beings. Vimalakīrti said:
"It is like a magician who sees the person created by his own illusion."
"The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being thus.
This is the second answer from Vimalakīrti.
There are two kinds of sentient beings:
If non-Buddhists recklessly speculate [on the existence of a self], it would be like the thirteen bases (āyatana) or even a smokeless fire; ultimately, such a sentient being does not exist.

Second, sentient beings are merely conventional designations based on causes and conditions and do not truly exist. Although they exist, they are non-existent; although non-existent, they exist. Therefore, the analogy of a magician observing his illusions is cited: as an illusion exists yet is non-existent, and though non-existent, it possesses form.
Question:
Can one also contemplate that nominally designated sentient beings are ultimately empty, as with the thirteen bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer:
Although provisional designations exist, they ultimately do not exist; from the perspective of their non-existence, this [example] may indeed serve as an analogy.

However, although sentient beings ultimately do not exist yet appear vividly as if they do, the analogy of the thirteen bases (*āyatana*) cannot be applied in the same way; therefore, it is not a complete parallel.

In this chapter, since sentient beings are seen to be like illusions, everything from the aforementioned inconceivable [nature] up to the illness of the Bodhisattva is likewise entirely like an illusion.

"Just as a wise person sees the moon in water, as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a mirror, as a shimmering mirage in the heat, as an echo, as clouds in the sky, as foam on the water, as bubbles upon the surface, as the solidity of a plantain tree, as lightning that lingers for a long time, as a fifth great element, as a sixth aggregate, as a seventh sense-organ, as the thirteenth base, and as the nineteenth realm—so does the Bodhisattva regard sentient beings."
Like an image within a mirror, it arises neither from itself nor from another, yet it does not exist without a cause;
for if it existed of itself, it would not depend upon the mirror,
and if it arose from another, it would not be produced by means of the face.
If it were without cause, it would not depend upon the surface of a mirror.
If one claims that although [the image] is entirely non-existent,
it nonetheless appears clearly as a form, the characteristics of sentient beings are analogous to this.

"Just as form in the formless realm, as a sprout from scorched grain, as the view of a self in the body of a stream-enterer, as the entry into a womb by a non-returner, as the three poisons in an arhat, as the greed, anger, and violation of precepts in a bodhisattva who has attained forbearance, as the habitual tendencies of affliction in a Buddha, as seeing forms by one who is blind, as inhalation and exhalation in one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation, as the tracks of a bird in the sky, as the son of a barren woman, as the afflictions of a transformed person, as that which is seen in a dream upon waking, as the taking up of a body by one who has entered parinirvāṇa, and as a fire without smoke—so does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings."
These various analogies all clarify the unity of existence and emptiness;
however, because those who cling to existence are numerous, they have been cited in full.

As for "form within the formless realm," according to the Mahāyāna, there is indeed form in the formless realm; the statement that it is "formless" is made by borrowing the terminology of the Hīnayāna as a metaphor.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, it is explained that the higher realms lack coarse matter; thus, "formless" (ārūpya) is said merely by borrowing the absence of coarse matter as a metaphor.

According to the meaning of the Abhidharma, regarding those who enter the womb as *anāgāmins*: although an *anāgāmin* may temporarily regress, they certainly do not undergo rebirth, and therefore they do not enter a womb within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
