Master Kumārajīva said: "When eating this rice, my body was at ease and my mind tranquil, giving rise to an unprecedented state of mind.
If even the rice is like this, how much more so must it be with the Way?"

"Since there is this wondrous fruit, there must be a wondrous cause. Through supreme faith and joy, and a profound understanding of cause and effect, one realizes that cause and effect are themselves dependent origination; by understanding dependent origination, one perceives the true nature of reality. It is for this reason that one attains the Way.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!"
"Thus, this fragrant meal is able to perform the work of a Buddha.
From here below is the second section, which fully clarifies the different ways in which the work of a Buddha is performed.
This is divided into two parts according to the text:
First, it correctly clarifies the manifold gates of the Buddha’s work; second, it explains that there is great benefit in understanding and entering these gates.
Regarding Ānanda’s exclamation: food fundamentally benefits the body, yet it ultimately enables one to attain the Way; therefore, he calls it "unprecedented."
"Buddha-activity" refers to the teaching and transformation of sentient beings, enabling them to realize the Way; this is indeed the work of all Buddhas.
"The Buddha said: 'So it is, so it is!'"
"Ānanda!
There are some buddha-fields where the Buddha’s work is accomplished through the light of the Buddha, and there are others where the Buddha’s work is accomplished by means of the bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: 'The Tathāgata remains silent, while the bodhisattvas preach the Dharma.'"
Furthermore, in this very sutra, while Śākyamuni remained silent, Vimalakīrti propagated the Way.
It is said that "there are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of a person emanated by the Buddha.
This is like the case of the Buddha Susaṃtata, whose true form entered parinirvāṇa, yet he left behind an emanation-buddha to benefit sentient beings.
"There are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of the Bodhi tree.
Because the Buddha attained bodhi beneath this tree, it is called the Bodhi tree.
This tree manifests forms and sounds according to what is seen and heard, enabling all to awaken to the Way; therefore, the tree performs the Buddha-work.
"Therefore, the Buddha performs the work of a Buddha through his robes and bedding.

Formerly, the King of Jambudvīpa obtained a great robe of the Buddha. At a time when there was a plague in the world, the king placed the robe atop a banner to show it to the multitude. The multitude took refuge in it, and all their illnesses were cured; their faith and reverence grew ever deeper, and by means of this, they attained liberation.
"There are those who perform Buddha-work through food and drink, and there are those who perform Buddha-work through gardens, groves, and palaces.
That the Land of Universal Fragrance uses fragrance as its ground and its parks to cause people to awaken to the Way is precisely such a case.
"There are those who perform the work of a Buddha by means of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; there are those who perform the work of a Buddha by means of the Buddha-body.
Or, they manifest their true form with its marks and characteristics, and thereby attain the Way.
Furthermore, it is like King Bimbisāra, who gave a Buddha image to King Pukkasāti and thereby attained awakening.
The "Buddha-body" refers to that which causes the manifestation of the body.
"There are those who perform deeds through emptiness, so that sentient beings may, by means of this condition, enter into the practice of discipline.
Because the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ: for those who prefer existence, they preserve their bodies to demonstrate existence;
for those who delight in emptiness, they extinguish their bodies to demonstrate non-existence."
Just as Mañjuśrī extinguished all forms and manifested the appearance of empty space in order to transform King Ajātaśatru,
as described in the *Guhyakapada Sūtra*.
“There are those who perform the work of a Buddha by means of such metaphors as a dream, an illusion, a reflection, an echo, an image in a mirror, the moon in water, and a mirage.”

There are sentient beings whom he causes to perceive dreams so that they may attain awakening; or there are those who receive benefit through the manifestation of illusions, mirages, and unreal forms and colors.

Some perform Buddha-work through sounds, speech, language, and written characters; others perform Buddha-work in pure buddha-fields that are silent, wordless, unspeakable, without demonstration, without cognition, and characterized by non-action and non-formation.
"It is thus, Ānanda!
In the majestic deportment and movements of all Buddhas, and in all their actions, there is nothing that is not Buddha-work.

There are true Buddha-lands where all are Dharma-body Bodhisattvas; externally they are without speech, and internally they are without conceptual thought, yet they attain awakening beyond phenomena by correctly contemplating the true mark and thereby attaining the Way.

“Ānanda! There are these four Māras and eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction, through which all sentient beings become exhausted; it is precisely by means of these dharmas that the Buddhas perform the work of a Buddha.”
Master Kumārajīva said: "There are three kinds of Buddha-activities:
first, performing Buddha-activities through the wholesome, such as preaching the Dharma and emitting light;
second, performing Buddha-activities through the indeterminate, such as empty space."
Third, taking what is unwholesome as a Buddha-work means manifesting all afflictions.
There are three grades of physicians:
those of the inferior grade may prepare medicine that becomes non-medicine;
Those of intermediate quality can take medicine as medicine;
superior physicians, however, use what is not medicine as medicine.
As for the eighty-four thousand [afflictions], they consist of the three poisons in equal measure.

These four are the roots of all afflictions; from each root emerge twenty-one thousand, totaling eighty-four thousand, because from these eighty-four thousand branch out immeasurable secondary streams.
Regarding what are called the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates, the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* records that a bodhisattva reflected:
"By practicing which samādhi can one swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand perfections?"
He therefore questioned the Buddha about this.
The Buddha replied that there is a samādhi called "Comprehending the Root of All Dharmas"; if a bodhisattva practices it, they will swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand pāramitās.

Regarding the various *pāramitās*: the Buddha’s merits consist of three hundred and fifty types of gates, each of which takes the six *pāramitās* as its cause; thus, there are two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*, which are employed to counteract the afflictions of the four great elements and the six decays.
The four great elements constitute the body of sentient beings; by practicing the various perfections (pāramitās), one attains the pure Dharma-body, and thus the four great elements are treated.
As for the six decays (ṣadāyatana), they are the evil thieves of the six sense-objects that cause a person’s wholesome dharmas to decline and perish;
by practicing the various perfections and entering the realm of the Buddha, one does not fear the six sense-objects, and thus they are treated.
The four great elements constitute the internal, and the six sense-bases constitute the external; since these internal and external factors arise from afflictions, they are to be remedied.
The three poisons and their equal combinations each consist of twenty-one thousand types, totaling eighty-four thousand.
"This is called the Dharma-door of entering into all Buddha-dharmas.
When a bodhisattva enters this door, if they see all pure and excellent buddha-fields, they do not feel joy, nor do they become greedy or conceited;
if they see all impure buddha-fields, they do not feel sorrow, nor are they hindered or discouraged."
Yet, they give rise to a pure mind toward all Buddha-fields, feeling joy and reverence as if it were something unprecedented.
The merits of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are equal; it is only for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings that they manifest different Buddha-fields.
"Ānanda!
You see that the lands of the various buddhas differ in their ground, yet space does not differ.
In this same way, you see that the form-bodies (rūpakāya) of the various buddhas differ, but their unimpeded wisdom (anāvaraṇajñāna) does not differ."
This second section clarifies how one enters this gate to obtain benefit.
It is divided into three parts according to the text:
first, the equality of virtue; second, the explanation of the names and so forth; third, the inability of the Hīnayāna to fathom it.
Virtues are likewise twofold:
first, clarifying the Buddha’s wisdom and so forth; second, distinguishing the remaining virtues and so forth. Regarding the Buddha’s wisdom and so forth:

once one has entered this gate, one realizes that the Buddha-lands are fundamentally manifestations in response to sentient beings; how then could the wisdom capable of such responding be anything other than identical?
Therefore, one gives rise to neither sorrow nor joy regarding purity or defilement. "Ānanda!

The physical bodies, majestic marks, lineage, precepts, concentration, wisdom, knowledge and vision of liberation, powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities, great kindness and great compassion, and the conduct of deportment of all Buddhas—as well as their lifespans, their preaching of the Dharma and teaching, their maturing of sentient beings, their purification of Buddha-lands, and their possession of all Buddha-dharmas—are entirely equal."
The aforementioned [qualities such as] supreme wisdom and so forth are now distinguished; all other virtues are identical.
Question:
Since the modes of transformation of the various Buddhas differ, how can they be said to be equal?
Answer:
All Buddhas equally possess all skillful means; therefore, they are equal.
"For this reason, he is called Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The former clarifies that their virtues are identical; this clarifies that their titles are equal.
However, these titles have many categories; briefly stated, there are three, which further expand to ten, and when fully enumerated, they are immeasurable.
This is now explained in brief.
This is the title of the first Samyaksaṃbuddha:

"Samyak" (Right) means being free from error; "Saṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened) means that wisdom is all-pervasive; and "Jñāna" (Knowledge) refers to the definitive realization of the characteristics of phenomena.
"He is named Tathāgata. This is translated as "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One), and is also called "Tathā-gata" (Thus-Gone).
Because he has come with a nature that is suchness, he is called "Tathāgata."
To depart according to the essence [of reality] is called "Thus-Gone" (Tathāgata).
Furthermore, because all Buddhas come in this manner, they are called "Thus-Come" (Tathāgata);
and because all Buddhas likewise enter nirvāṇa and depart, it is called "Thus-Gone."
"Buddha" is the name;
this translates as "Awakened.
There are two kinds of awakening:
First, awakening from the slumber of the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa), which is common to the two vehicles;
second, awakening from the slumber of the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa), which distinguishes them from the two vehicles.
The afflictive hindrance refers to the afflictions of the four stages of dwelling.
The cognitive hindrance is that which obstructs the Tathāgata’s omniscience; it is the delusion of the stage of ignorance-dwelling.
"Ānanda!..."

If I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail, you would not be able to receive it all even with a lifespan of an eon; even if all the sentient beings filling the great trichiliocosm were like Ānanda, foremost in much-hearing and possessing mindfulness and dhāraṇī, these people together would still not be able to receive it even with a lifespan of an eon.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is without limit; their wisdom and eloquence are inconceivable.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"From this day forward, I shall not dare to call myself one of great learning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Do not give rise to thoughts of retreat! Why is this?
I have declared that among the śrāvakas you are the most learned, but I did not say this of a bodhisattva.
"Stop, Ānanda!
One who possesses wisdom should not attempt to limit the measure of bodhisattvas.
While all the deep oceans may still be measured, the spiritual powers, wisdom, eloquence, dhāraṇīs, and all the meritorious virtues of a bodhisattva are immeasurable."
"Ānanda!

Set aside for a moment the practices of bodhisattvas; the supernatural power manifested by Vimalakīrti in a single instant is something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas could not achieve even by exerting their full transformative powers throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
Third, as for their virtues or names, they cannot be fathomed by those of the Hīnayāna; this collectively reveals that all Buddhas are inconceivable.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the World of Universal Fragrance joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"When we first saw this land, we conceived an inferior notion of it; now we repent and reproach ourselves, having abandoned such a mind. Why is this?
The skillful means of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they manifest various Buddha-lands according to what is appropriate for each."
This second section, concerning the Bodhisattva Sarvagandhasugandha returning to his own land, consists of three parts according to the text:
first, the request; second, the teaching; and third, the realization.
The first part contains two sentences:
First, repentance for one's own transgressions; second, requesting the Dharma.

Regarding repentance for one's own transgressions: although one has set out for that land and followed the holy teachings, upon seeing the impurity of this land, inferior conceptions naturally arise, leading one to think that even Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have degrees of superiority and inferiority.
Only after hearing of these Buddha-activities does one finally repent and reproach oneself.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you grant us a small portion of the Dharma, so that upon returning to our own land, we may keep the Tathāgata in mind."
Second, there are five causes and conditions for all dharmas:

First, although this [land] possesses written words, it requires those [dharmas], and although that [land] is without speech, it also requires these dharmas; thus, as the transformative influence spreads between the two nations, they mutually benefit one another.
Second, since one is already a bodhisattva, one must universally transform the ten directions; therefore, one requests written words to instruct and guide other lands.

Third, there are those in the World of Various Fragrances who have not yet come; they will surely inquire about the essential meaning, and thus it is necessary to transmit this alternative teaching like a lamp being passed on.

Fourth, it causes those bodhisattvas to realize the Buddha’s grace: having attained awakening to the Way simply by eating fragrant food, they will now understand that they only ascend to the state of a sage upon hearing of such ascetic practices, thereby recognizing the depth of the Buddha’s kindness and exhorting themselves to cultivate virtue.
Fifth, although the instruction was given for their sake, the underlying intention was actually for this purpose.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"There is a dharma-gate of liberation called 'the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible'; you all should study it.
This second Buddha is further divided into three parts:
First, the two gates are presented to encourage study; second, the two gates are explained to clarify the encouragement; third, the two gates are concluded to finalize the encouragement.
This is the initial presentation.
"What is meant by 'exhaustion'?"
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). What are inexhaustible?
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
This explains two gates:
conditioned phenomena are false and must inevitably undergo destruction, and are thus called "conditioned";
unconditioned phenomena are real and cannot be destroyed, and are therefore named "unconditioned."
The preceding two phrases indicate the dharmas to be studied:
"As for the bodhisattva, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The following clarifies the two gates through which one is able to study.
Furthermore, there are three phrases:
first, a general indication of the two practices; second, a detailed explanation of the two practices; and third, a combined interpretation of the two practices.
Regarding the fact that one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are two gates:
First, one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), entering the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in order to transform sentient beings;
yet one does not abide in the unconditioned—this is skillful means (*upāya*) and does not mean realizing emptiness.
This represents abandoning the unconditioned to enter the conditioned, used to refute the Śrāvakas who abide in the unconditioned and abandon the conditioned.
Second, the defiled land possesses suffering and is therefore called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*);
the pure land is free from suffering and is thus termed "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
That the Bodhisattva Saugandhika delights in the pure land and abandons the defiled land is precisely to relinquish the conditioned and dwell in the unconditioned.
Now, by rebuking him here, it is clarified that one does not dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor abandon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Previously, the Śrāvakas were censured; now, the Bodhisattvas are rebuked.
However, those in the Pure Land truly possess no such fault; this is merely a case of using them as a vehicle to censure the present subject.
"What is meant by not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
It means not being separated from great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and not abandoning great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This provides a detailed explanation of two gates, which constitutes two meanings.

Now, first, regarding the "Great Being who does not exhaust the conditioned": because he takes the salvation of sentient beings as his concern, entering into the conditioned world to transform beings is the fundamental intention of a Bodhisattva; therefore, it was explained previously that he does not exhaust the conditioned.

Compassion is the foundation for entering the Way and the root for cultivating virtue; therefore, it is clarified at the very outset. The Śrāvakas lack this, and thus they abide in the inexhaustible realm of conditioned existence.
"Profoundly generating the mind of omniscience and never forgetting it.
The former refers to the mind that delivers sentient beings; the latter refers to the mind that seeks the Buddha-way, which is also the mind of great vows.

Furthermore, because the heart of this Bodhicitta-tree is deep and firm, it is difficult to topple or destroy; thus, throughout kalpas, it becomes ever more luminous without falling into negligence or delusion.
One never grows weary of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
regarding the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one constantly reflects upon and practices them in accordance with them.
"To uphold the True Dharma without sparing one's own body or life,
and to cultivate all roots of goodness without weariness—
these two, which provide succor to sentient beings below and seek the Buddha-way above, are the root of all virtues."
However, "transforming and teaching sentient beings" and "practicing the four means of integration" constitute the former aspect of downward succor;
"protecting the true Dharma" and "planting roots of goodness" constitute the former aspect of upward seeking.
With these manifold virtues flourishing upon its branches and twigs, the Tree of the Way grows daily more luxuriant; this does not exhaust the meaning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
All subsequent streams of vows and practices, like its branches and leaves, may likewise flourish, thereby fulfilling the principle of inexhaustibility.
"The will always abides securely, and through skillful means, it is dedicated [to enlightenment].

The practice of goodness is not fixed; it is accomplished according to one's intention. If one possesses skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the path of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one does not follow the three realms of existence or the two vehicles, but swiftly attains perfect awakening; therefore, the mind must always abide securely.
"Seeking the Dharma without indolence and preaching it without parsimony, diligently making offerings to all Buddhas, one enters the cycle of birth and death without fear.
Regarding all honors and insults, the mind remains free from sorrow or joy;
one does not slight those who have not yet studied, but respects those who do as if they were Buddhas."
Regarding the secondary afflictions, they cause one to give rise to right mindfulness;
they do not regard the pleasure of seclusion as precious,
nor do they cling to their own pleasure, but instead rejoice in the pleasure of others.

Ordinary beings feel aversion when they see others' happiness and find peace of mind when they see others' suffering; they become attached when they experience their own happiness and feel weary when they experience their own suffering.

Bodhisattvas, however, rejoice when they see others' happiness and give rise to compassion when they see others' suffering; they do not become attached when they experience their own happiness and find peace of mind when they experience their own suffering.
"In all meditative concentrations (dhyāna), one should maintain the perception of them as being like hell.
There are three types of dhyāna:
first, that of the Mahāyāna; second, that of the Hīnayāna; and third, that of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
The dhyāna of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) frequently gives rise to conceit (*asmimāna*);

the dhyāna of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), however, is self-centered, which burns away their wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) and destroys the tree of the Buddha; therefore, they view it as being like hell.
"Regarding birth and death, one should conceive of them as a pleasure garden.
Although birth and death are suffering, they are the cause for the Great Path; the Bodhisattva delights in wandering therein, conceiving of it as a pleasure garden.
"When seeing those who come seeking [help], one should regard them as a good teacher.
Although the seekers desire to benefit themselves, they actually benefit me; therefore, one should regard them as a good teacher.
"Renounce all that one possesses, maintaining the perception of universal wisdom;
when seeing those who violate the precepts, give rise to the perception of providing protection;
and regard the various pāramitās as one's parents."
The first phrase clarifies giving (*dāna*): it means that by relinquishing one’s body and life to the thief [of afflictions], one will certainly be able to attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The second phrase distinguishes ethical discipline (*śīla*): discipline serves as protection for a person; if one violates the precepts, there is no protection.
Because the Bodhisattva himself possesses protection, this protection is for those who lack it.
The latter phrase refers to the four pāramitās; as their practice becomes increasingly profound, they become the source from which the Dharma-body arises, and are thus conceived of as parents.
"Regarding the dharmas of the *mārga-varga*, one should conceive of them as kinsmen.
Those factors that assist and benefit me—the thirty-seven [auxiliaries]—are like a person who achieves success through the assistance of their kinsmen.
"Planting roots of goodness without limit;
completing the adornment of Buddha-lands through the perfection of the embellishments of all pure lands;
practicing boundless giving to be fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks."
"Eliminating all evils and purifying body, speech, and mind.

Thus, some may have little but their hearts are sufficient, while others may have sufficient wealth but their hearts are meager; now, as both matters are present together, he is able to open his doors for great giving.
This giving is the cause of the primary and secondary marks; when practicing this giving, one must purify the three karmas.
Since the cause is purified, the wondrous retribution will necessarily follow.
"Throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, their minds remain courageous;
hearing of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues, their resolve never tires;
with the sword of wisdom, they slay the thieves of affliction."
Transcending the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, they bear the burden of sentient beings, ensuring their eternal liberation.
With great diligence, they subdue the armies of Māra and constantly seek the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptuality.
To give rise to no perverse thoughts regarding the four propositions of existence and non-existence is true wisdom.
"To practice few desires and contentment without abandoning worldly dharmas;
to not violate dignified deportment while being able to conform to worldly customs;"
"Without violating the protocols of the Path, one can nevertheless conform to worldly customs.
Looking up and down across the world, everyone says, "I am the same as them," yet I alone am a person who is different.
"Arising the wisdom of supernatural powers, one guides sentient beings;"
Attaining the dhāraṇī of mindfulness, they do not forget what they have heard;
skillfully discerning the various faculties, they sever the doubts of sentient beings;
and through the eloquence of joyful speech, they expound the Dharma without obstruction.
By purifying the ten paths of wholesome action, one receives the blessings of devas and humans;
by cultivating the four immeasurables, one opens the way to the Brahma-heavens;
by exhorting others to preach the Dharma, rejoicing in it, and praising its excellence, one attains the melodic voice of a Buddha.
With excellence of body, speech, and mind, they attain the majestic deportment of a Buddha; deeply cultivating wholesome dharmas, their practice becomes ever more sublime.
By virtue of the Mahāyāna teachings, they become the community of Bodhisattvas, remaining free from negligence and never losing any of their manifold virtues.
Practicing these dharmas as described above is called "the Bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of the conditioned.
Being able to thus practice for oneself and transform others, one's merit increases daily; this is what is meant by not exhausting the conditioned.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in the unconditioned?
It means training in emptiness, yet not taking emptiness as a realization;
training in signlessness and wishlessness, yet not taking signlessness and wishlessness as realizations."
This explains "not abiding in the unconditioned": by means of the wisdom of skillful means, one contemplates emptiness without realizing it; this is called "not abiding in the unconditioned.
Question:
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles distinguish the three types of emptiness; what is their difference?
Answer:
The contemplation of emptiness in the Two Vehicles is empty only of a self;
the contemplation of emptiness in the Mahāyāna is such that there is no phenomenon that is not empty.
Since no dharma is not empty, even the dharma of emptiness is empty;
because the dharma of emptiness is also empty, one is thus able to not realize emptiness.
The signlessness of the Hīnayāna consists only of the truth of cessation, whereas the Mahāyāna is free from all signs.
The non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) of the Hīnayāna does not create birth-and-death;
the non-action of the Mahāyāna does not create any phenomena (*dharmas*).
"One practices and studies non-arising, yet one does not take non-arising as a realization."
Sengzhao said: "All phenomena exist when conditions converge and cease to exist when conditions disperse.
What phenomenon could have existed beforehand, waiting for conditions to arise?
This is a specific gateway to the contemplation of emptiness."

Some say: the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is "emptiness"; the absence of any characteristic of emptiness that can be grasped is "signlessness"; the absence of anything produced as a result is "wishlessness"; and the absence of any cause from which they could arise is "non-arising."

"Contemplating impermanence yet not wearying of the roots of goodness; contemplating impermanence merely as an antidote to the notion of permanence—how could one allow for annihilationism by failing to practice the roots of goodness?
'Contemplating the suffering of the world yet not loathing birth and death;
contemplating non-self yet teaching others without weariness.'"
To contemplate non-self is what is meant by the emptiness of persons;
though empty, it exists, and thus one teaches others without weariness.
To contemplate quiescent extinction, yet not to enter into eternal extinction;
"One contemplates seclusion and cultivates goodness in body and mind.
There are three kinds of seclusion: first, distancing oneself from the five desires; [the other two follow].
Second, being free from afflictions;

third, the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) and the state of being utterly remote and detached—this is another name for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Although one perceives the peace of this unconditioned detachment, body and mind do not depart from conditioned goodness (*saṃskṛta-kuśala*).
"Observing that there is nowhere to which one returns, yet returning to and taking refuge in wholesome dharmas.

All dharmas have no place from which they come at the beginning and no place to which they return at the end; although one knows there is no place of return, one constantly returns to wholesome dharmas.
“Contemplating non-arising, yet bearing the burden of all phenomena through the dharma of arising;
contemplating the outflow-free, yet not severing the various outflows.
To contemplate the outflow-free is to differ from ordinary beings.
He manifests the practice of outflows, and thus it is said that he does not sever them, distinguishing him from those of the Two Vehicles.
He contemplates the absence of anything to be practiced, yet employs the practice of the Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings;
he contemplates emptiness and non-existence, yet does not abandon great compassion.

"Contemplating the stage of the True Dharma, yet not following the Lesser Vehicle; contemplating all phenomena as illusory, without solidity, without a self, without birth, and without marks; yet, while his original vows are not yet fulfilled, he does not let his merit, meditative concentration, or wisdom go to waste."
Nevertheless, although one knows that all phenomena are without self and without master, one does not fail to cultivate them because they are provisional and empty of merit.
To cultivate such dharmas is called "the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned."
In summary, this means not abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Furthermore, because they possess merit, they do not abide in the unconditioned;
because they possess wisdom, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)"—the following section is the third part, which combines and explains these two lines.
Although the preceding section clarified that [the Buddha] is neither exhaustive nor abiding, it now provides a comprehensive explanation thereof.
Cultivating merit and virtue necessarily involves the realm of existence; if one were to abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then merit and virtue would not be fully realized.
Because they possess wisdom, they know that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are like illusions and do not allow themselves to become defiled by or attached to them;

therefore, they do not exhaust conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, the nature of wisdom necessarily illuminates all dharmas universally; if one were to abandon conditioned phenomena, then wisdom would not be complete.
"Because of great compassion, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
From this point downward, the first pair—merit and wisdom—is the general [category], which also constitutes self-benefit;
from here downward, the three pairs are the specific [categories], which further constitute the benefit of others.
Compassion and the original vow specifically open the gate of merit.
Within this gate of merit, there are both vows and practice; compassion constitutes its virtue.

The latter phrase refers to the vow: by cultivating compassion, one turns back from non-existence to enter into existence. Because the vow is fulfilled, one neither dwells [in existence] nor exhausts [it].
"Because they gather the medicine of the Dharma, they do not abide in the unconditioned;
because they administer the medicine according to [the patient's needs], they do not exhaust the conditioned.
The following two pairs open the gates of wisdom.
The former concerns the gathering of medicine, while the latter concerns the diagnosis of the illness.
However, since the gathering of medicine must necessarily derive from a teacher, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
for if one were to abandon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it would cause sentient beings to be cut off [from the means of healing], so how could one administer the medicine?
Therefore, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
"Because one knows the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not abide in the unconditioned;
because one extinguishes the illnesses of sentient beings, one does not exhaust the conditioned."
Knowing the illnesses of sentient beings, one must necessarily illumine existence; therefore, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings, one must enter into existence; therefore, one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
“O noble sons!
When a bodhisattva has cultivated this dharma, they do not exhaust the conditioned nor do they abide in the unconditioned; this is called the unimpeded dharma-gate of exhaustion and non-exhaustion.”
"From 'You all should train' onwards, this third section summarizes the two gates to encourage study.
The section on 'exhaustion and non-exhaustion' summarizes the essence of the dharmas to be studied, while the section on the 'unobstructed dharma-gate' summarizes the practice of those who study."

Because one does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while remaining free from the burden of lacking virtues, and does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while being free from the limitation of solitary self-benefit, it is called "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*).
Question:
Since not exhausting the conditioned also carries the sense of "exhausting," and since not abiding in the unconditioned also carries the sense of "abiding," is this so?
Answer:
When a bodhisattva relinquishes the two kinds of birth-and-death, they exhaust the conditioned;
when they realize great nirvana, they abide in the unconditioned.
What was previously called "not exhausting" means causing those who transform sentient beings to enter [the path];
"not abiding" means not being the same as the two vehicles in seeking realization.

At that time, when those bodhisattvas heard this Dharma being preached, they were all greatly rejoiced. With various wonderful flowers of many colors and many fragrances, they scattered them throughout the trichiliocosm to make offerings to the Buddha, to this sutra and its Dharma, and to all the bodhisattvas. Having done so, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, marveled at what had never occurred before, and said:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is indeed able to employ such skillful means here!
Having said this, he suddenly vanished and returned to his own land.
This was the third understanding.
Rejoicing and praising him, they returned to their own lands. 12.
Chapter Twelve: Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya (6). Regarding the chapter "Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," *Akṣobhya* means "Immovable" in this language, and is also named "Without Anger."
Previously, names were established based on the Dharma; now, titles are received according to the person.
Furthermore, the former was a name based on causes, while the present is a cause for the fruit.
Moreover, in the previous case, both the person and the Dharma were raised together: the Bodhisattva is the person, and their practice is the Dharma.
Now, this title signifies the simultaneous possession of both object and wisdom: "View" refers to the wisdom that is the subject of contemplation, while Akṣobhya is the object of contemplation.
Question:
For what reason does this chapter exist?
Answer:
There are four meanings in total.

First, previously this teaching was expounded for the sake of that land, whereas now, for these specific conditions, one contemplates that Buddha; this is truly because the ways of receiving awakening differ, and the gates of transformation are not uniform.
2. In the preceding "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," the cultivation of practice was distinguished; now, the perfection of that practice is clarified, whereby one is able to see the Buddha.
Question:
Since the followers of the Two Vehicles also see that Buddha, they too should cultivate the practices of a Buddha.
Answer:
They see only the Buddha of the Two Vehicles, not the true Buddha.

Thus, when the five hundred śrāvakas sat in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, they saw only a Buddha sixteen feet tall, identical in stature to the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles; because they had cultivated distinct roots of goodness, they did not perceive the true Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna.
Third, whereas the preceding section explained the gate of causes, this section clarifies the dharma of the fruit; fourth,
from the beginning of this sutra up to this point, the inconceivable has been briefly distinguished,
while from this passage onward, the fundamental and the manifested, which are difficult to fathom, will be explained in detail.
Contemplating the true mark of the body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way; this is called the inconceivability of the fundamental.
Next, the explanation of the relocation of Abhirati to enter this land is called the inconceivability of the trace.
Question:
Since the inconceivable has already been clarified above, how does it differ from the present case?
Answer:
To provide a general judgment on the beginning and end, there are four propositions:
first, the inconceivable entry of the great into the small, such as borrowing a seat from King Dīpaṃkara;
second, the inconceivable filling of the small by the great, such as requesting a meal from the Fragrant Land.

Third, by means of the great entering the great inconceivable, he transported that Land of Wonderful Joy into this Saha World; the two lands coexisted without increase or decrease, which is called the inconceivable.
However, this matter is easy to understand and requires no further explanation.
This chapter is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the essence of the Dharmakāya;
Second, distinguishing the traceless state of immovability;
third, praising the Dharma and its practitioners.
Regarding the first [the father], there is first the question and then the answer.
"At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti:
'If you wish to see the Tathāgata, by what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata? Below this, the Buddha’s inquiry to Vimalakīrti contains three general meanings:

First, from the beginning of the sutra until now, whenever the Buddha’s body emitted radiance or his voice resounded, the assembly merely perceived the marks of a human being and failed to see the Dharma-body; therefore, he questions Vimalakīrti to cause them to behold the true Buddha.

Second, regarding the "Purity of the Superior," it is said that one can see the Buddhas. At that time, the assembly thought that the Buddha could be seen and that there were people capable of seeing him.
If this were so, it would still be the Buddha who sees, rather than [the assembly] seeing the Buddha.
Therefore, we now clarify the Dharma-body to bring those two types of contemplation to rest.
Question:
When the Bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance came to see the Buddha, they also gave rise to delusions and attachments; why did [the Buddha] not refute them?
Answer:
Since he gives rise to an inferior conception, how could defilement arise?
Therefore, it is said only in relation to his departure.

Third, because he wished to clarify that there is no distinction between superior and inferior, and fearing that there might arise dualistic thoughts of superiority and inferiority regarding the coming of the Immovable Buddha alongside Śākyamuni, he preemptively clarified the single contemplation of the Dharmakāya; this is why he asked.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Just as one contemplates the true reality of one's own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha. Below this is the answer.
Question:
In these four assemblies of this sutra, the Dharma-body is elucidated in three locations; what is the difference between them?
Answer:
In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the merits of the Dharma-body are extolled in contrast to the faults and afflictions of birth-and-death.

In the "Chapter on Disciples," the distinction between the Revealed (迹) and the Origin (本) is opened: while the Dharma-body is untainted and unconditioned, its manifested traces are subject to birth and extinction.
This chapter specifically clarifies that the essence of the Dharma-body transcends the hundred negations, yet its form is fully endowed with the myriad virtues.
Question:
For what reason are these three gates distinguished?
Answer:
One must prepare for three gates for the Buddha-body to become manifest.
First, one must contrast the faults and afflictions of birth and death with the merits of the Dharma-body, causing one to weary of this birth and death and to joyfully seek the Buddha-body.
The doubters may now think: "The Buddha’s body we see is still conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and has not yet escaped the outflows (*āsrava*); how is it worth rejoicing in?

Therefore, the second chapter opens with the distinction between the fundamental and the manifested: that which is conditioned and subject to outflows is merely the manifested trace (*nirmāṇa-niṣyanda*);
only that which is unconditioned and free from outflows is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Alternatively, one might hear that the Dharma-body is such that all afflictions are exhausted and all virtues are perfected, and thus claim it is different from sentient beings.
For this reason, this chapter clarifies that in contemplating the true mark of the body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way; there is no duality between sentient beings and the Buddha.
When these three gates are possessed, the meaning is complete; it not only provides immediate access to this specific section but also remotely penetrates all the various scriptures.
Furthermore, it first refutes the ordinary person, next censures the two vehicles, and finally instructs the bodhisattvas.

First, regarding those addressed as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): because ordinary beings inquire about illness in the "Expedient Means" chapter, [the Buddha] preaches for them the faults and afflictions of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the merits of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Next, in the "Disciples" chapter, he directly rebukes the Śrāvakas, asserting that the Buddha’s body is identical to that of the Two Vehicles; therefore, he reveals the distinction between their original and manifested traces (*honji-suijaku*).

The Bodhisattva identifies with the Buddha-body, perceiving that it is eternally abiding yet arises and ceases with sovereign mastery over sentient beings; thus, he now manifests the true reality (dharmatā) of the body, and his contemplation of the Buddha is likewise so, thereby submerging the two [dualistic] views.
Master Kumārajīva said: "There are three ways of contemplating the Buddha:
first, contemplating his physical form; second, contemplating the Dharma-body; and third, contemplating the emptiness of nature.

Among these three gates of contemplation, Vimalakīrti employs the gate of the emptiness of nature in his response; therefore, it is said: 'Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha in the same way.'"
Now, it is said that this chapter precisely elucidates the meaning of the nature-emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)—that the Dharma-body transcends the four propositions and the hundred negations.
Question:
In what sense is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) itself the Buddha-body?
Answer:
The Buddha’s body transcends the four propositions, and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings likewise transcends the four propositions; therefore, true reality is itself the Dharma-body.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "As there is no coming or going, suchness (*tathatā*) is itself the Buddha."
Question:
Since *tathatā* (suchness) and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are the objects of contemplation for the True Dharma, how can they be the spiritual wisdom of the Buddha?
Answer:
One who poses such a question is merely following their own subjective mind; it is not the language of the sūtras or śāstras. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. The *Tattvasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "It is also called Suchness, the Dharma-nature, and Nirvāṇa. How could one say that Nirvāṇa is also without cognition?
Therefore, the Dharmakāya is without cognition, yet there is nothing it does not know; this is also true according to the meaning [of the term].
Question:
If one contemplates the true mark of the body and contemplates the Buddha in the same way, how can this be called "seeing the Buddha"?
Answer:
To say that the Buddha is different from his body constitutes the two views; this is not seeing the Buddha.
Only by attaining the non-dual contemplation is one said to see the Buddha.

"Observing the Tathāgata, I see that he does not come from the past, does not go to the future, and does not abide in the present. From this point downward, this fully explains how the Dharma-body is utterly free from the hundred negations and is endowed with the myriad virtues.
This first phrase, clarifying that [the Dharma-body] does not belong to the three periods of time, intends to distinguish the Dharma-body from being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Ordinary beings, being conditioned, necessarily fall within the three periods;
since it does not belong to the three periods, it is therefore not conditioned.
"Neither observing form, nor observing the suchness of form, nor observing the nature of form;

neither observing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor observing the suchness of consciousness, nor observing the nature of consciousness"—since the five aggregates are also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the text next clarifies that they are not the Dharma-body by means of these five aggregates.
Regarding each individual aggregate (*skandha*), there are three modes of contemplation:
first, not contemplating form is the non-existence contemplation;
second, not contemplating the suchness of form is the non-emptiness contemplation.
Third, one does not contemplate the nature of form, thereby dispelling [the notions of] neither existence nor non-existence.
Since the Dharma-body transcends the four propositions, one likewise does not contemplate neither existence nor non-existence.

"Arising not from the four great elements, it is identical to empty space. Below this, the five aggregates are the effect and the four great elements are the cause; since the effect is not the Buddha, the cause is likewise not so.
Being neither cause nor effect, it is identical to empty space.

Regarding the passage "the six sense bases have no accumulation" and below: since the Dharma-body is neither cause nor effect, it also transcends the internal and external. Because it is neither external nor internal, the six sense bases cannot be accumulated; rather, they constitute Buddhahood as they are.

The passage beginning with "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already transcended" first clarifies that [the Tathāgata] is not among the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*); this section distinguishes his transcendence of internal nature.

The passage beginning with "He does not abide within the three realms" addresses the following: having already transcended the six sense bases mentioned above, one might suppose he abides where the six sense bases exist, or perhaps where they do not; therefore, it further states that he does not abide within the three realms.

"Having already abandoned the three impurities" and below: the preceding section clarified the absence of the fruits of the three realms; this section distinguishes the absence of the causes of the three realms.
Because the three impurities do not exist, one does not abide within the three realms.
From the six preceding sections, it was clarified that the Tathāgata is free from all delusions.
From the section "In accordance with the three gates of liberation" onwards, this clarifies that the Dharmakāya is endowed with all virtues.
Because one accords with the three gates of liberation, one is free from the three defilements.
Regarding the phrase "the three knowledges, ignorance, and so forth," there are two types of the three knowledges:
first, the three consisting of the divine eye, knowledge of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows; [and second, the three knowledges of the noble ones].
Second, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
first, the "wisdom of the bodhisattva," which refers to *prajñā*;
second, the "eye of the Buddhas," which is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
Third, non-ignorance (amoha), which refers to ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā).
Ultimate emptiness is not of the nature of wisdom (prajñā) in its essence, and therefore it is not "knowledge" (vidyā);
yet, because it can give rise to true wisdom, it is called "knowledge."

Just as the five sensory objects give rise to the five desires, these too are called "desires"; because they accord with the three gates of liberation, they can clarify [the distinction between] illumination and non-illumination.
Alternatively, it may be said that the three gates of liberation are themselves illumination; therefore, they are subsequently extinguished.
This is why it clarifies that ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are equal.
Regarding the passage "neither of one aspect nor of different aspects," Master Sengzhao says: "Because there is no form that is not form, they cannot be considered one;
because there is form yet no form, they cannot be considered different."
Regarding the connection with the "arising of the superior," [the text] clarifies that ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are treated as one;
yet if they were not one, they would follow the characteristics of difference. Therefore, it is now clarified that they are neither identical nor different.

Regarding the passage "not by its own characteristics, not by the characteristics of another": the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is "not by itself" because it arises through the resonance of sentient beings; the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is "not by another" because its essence is quiescent.
Sengzhao said: "Not by itself yet identical with itself, therefore it is itself yet not itself;
not by another yet identical with another, therefore it is another yet not another."
"How can the body of signlessness be observed in terms of self and other?
"It is neither signless nor characterized by grasping at signs. Below this, it is said that because it accords with the activities of others, it is not signless;
yet because its virtuous essence is eternally quiescent and devoid of discrimination, it is not characterized by grasping at signs.
This explanation is based on the synthesis of the two bodies (kāya).
Sengzhao stated, "It is not the mark of non-existence, nor is it a mark that can be grasped," which explains it solely from the perspective of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
"Neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor the middle stream": because birth and death are fundamentally non-existent, it is not "this shore";
because nirvana does not currently exist [as a fixed entity], it is not "the other shore."
Since there is neither "this" nor "that," how could there be an "eightfold middle stream"?

Furthermore, because one constantly dwells within birth and death, one does not go "there"; because one does not abandon nirvana, one does not come "here. Practicing both paths simultaneously without partial attachment, one thus does not abide in a middle stream.

Regarding the phrase "and transforms sentient beings," the previous statement that they are "not three" might suggest that transformative activity has ceased; therefore, it is now said that although they are not three, they constantly teach and transform others, causing them to realize that they are not three.

Regarding the passage, "Contemplating quiescence, yet not being eternally extinguished": since it speaks of transforming sentient beings below, it might appear that there are sentient beings to be seen, which would contradict quiescence.
Therefore, it is now clarified that although one transforms others, one remains eternally quiescent; thus it says, "contemplating quiescence.
Furthermore, although one is quiescent, one constantly teaches and transforms others; therefore, it is not an eternal extinction.
Regarding the phrase "neither here nor there": once one has transformed sentient beings, one exists in terms of "here" and "there.
Because the Dharma-body is without marks, it does not exist in terms of "here" or "there."
Furthermore, all lands are thus; since there is nothing that can be "this," it is called "not this";
since there is nothing that can be "that," it is said to be "not that.
Regarding the passage "neither by this nor by that": because it is not this yet is identical to this, it is "this" and yet "not this."
Not being that, yet being identical to that; therefore, being that, yet not being that—how could one then again use this to be identical to this, or use that to be identical to that?
This is because it clarifies that the Sage’s mind is a mind without a mind, by which he brings all minds into accord.

"Cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. Below this, it means that the ten wisdoms (*jñāna*) of the sages do not know it, and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) of ordinary beings do not cognize it.
The arising of ordinary wisdom and consciousness occurs within the realm of marks (*nimitta*);
since the Dharma-body is without marks, wisdom and consciousness cannot reach it.
Regarding the passage "Neither dark nor bright": because the Dharma-body has no cognition, it is not "bright";
because there is nothing it does not know, it is not "dark.
Regarding the passage "Neither name nor mark": it cannot be named by names, nor can it be characterized by marks; therefore, squares and circles cannot depict it, and titles cannot transmit it.
Regarding the phrase "neither strong nor weak": because the ultimate softness encounters no opposition, it is not rigid; because rigidity subdues all things, it is not weak.
Furthermore, though it moves heaven and earth, it is not rigid; though it responds to the exhaustion of impermanence, it is not weak.
Regarding the phrase "neither pure nor defiled": because there is no impurity that is not exhausted, it is not defiled;
because there is no fruition that is not attained, it is not pure.
Furthermore, the adornment of the body with the marks and signs of excellence does not constitute its purity.
The "Golden Spear" and "Horse-Grain" [incidents] were likewise not defilements.
Regarding the phrase "not abiding in a direction yet not departing from a direction": it is wondrously not within the triple world, and thus does not abide in a direction;
yet because there is no delusion to which it does not respond, it does not depart from a direction.
Regarding the phrase "neither conditioned nor unconditioned": because its characteristics cannot be altered, it is not conditioned;
because its wondrous function is inexhaustible, it is not unconditioned.
Regarding the phrase "no showing and no teaching" below: since the six sense-faculties cannot reach it, how could it be taught to others by means of speech?
To address people with words is "showing," and to rely on the Dharma through words is "teaching."
Furthermore, that which should be seen is shown, and that which should be heard is explained.
Yet, because the Buddha cannot be seen or heard, there is neither explanation nor demonstration.

From the passage "no giving and no stinginess, no precepts and no violation, no patience and no anger, no diligence and no indolence, no concentration and no distraction, no wisdom and no folly" onwards, these take the six perfections as their essence; therefore, they respond like an echo.
As for what is called "those who should be delivered," it means not delivering them by way of form (*rūpa*); there is neither deliverance nor non-deliverance, and only then is there deliverance.
Regarding the phrase "not insincere and not deceptive": "sincere" (*cheng*) means reality.
"Deception" means to delude.
Because one cannot treat the good as good, one is insincere;
because one cannot treat the evil as evil, one is not deceptive.
Furthermore, because the three matters were previously wasted in vain, it is not insincere;
because one has now finally attained that which was sought, it is not deceptive.

Regarding the passage "neither coming nor going, neither exiting nor entering": arriving by means of the path of reality is "coming"; the Sugata’s entry into parinirvāṇa is "going"; rushing in alarm toward the burning house is "entering"; standing outside the gate is "exiting"—yet in truth, the Dharma-body is none of these.
The phrase "All paths of language are cut off" below summarizes the preceding statements to demonstrate that [the nature of reality] is ineffable.

Regarding the passage "Neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings": one incurs fault by treating it with pride, hence it is not a field of merit;
one gains merit by honoring it with reverence, hence it is not a non-field of merit.
If it is not a field of merit, one should not make offerings;
if it is a field of merit, one should make offerings.
Some people say:
The Dharma-body has nothing that it receives, and thus it is not a field of merit;
yet it accepts offerings in response to sentient beings, and thus it is not a non-field of merit.
Furthermore, because it is not the same as ordinary virtuous persons, it is not a field of merit.
Because they are not like ordinary sinners, they are not non-fields of merit.
"Neither grasping nor abandoning": because it is not merit, there is no grasping; because it is not demerit, there is no abandoning.
It is not that it is not a field of merit; therefore, it is not "abandonment.

Regarding the phrase "neither with marks nor without marks": it is "not with marks" because it is quiescent, formless, and without shape; it is "not without marks" because it possesses the thirty-two marks.

Regarding the passage "identical with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)": the Dharma-body is without marks, and this is precisely the limit of reality; however, because some might consider the Buddha to be distinct [from it], the text says they are "identical."
"Beyond measure and beyond calculation, surpassing all measures and calculations": because its essence is neither light nor heavy, it cannot be weighed;
because its boundaries and manifestations are unfathomable, it cannot be measured.
Regarding the phrase "neither large nor small": it is larger than heaven and earth, so it cannot be called small;
it enters the infinitesimal gaps of space, so it cannot be called large.
That which can be both large and small is that which possesses neither largeness nor smallness.

Regarding the passage "neither seen nor heard, neither sensed nor known": it is not seen because it is not form; it is not heard because it is not sound; it is not sensed by the three [faculties of] smell, taste, or touch because it is not odor, flavor, or tangibility; and it is not known by the mind because it is not a mental object (*dharma*).
"Free from all fetters and bonds": since this is neither seen, heard, sensed, nor known, from what could fetters and bonds arise?

"Equal to all wisdoms and identical to sentient beings, one has no discrimination regarding all phenomena. Herein, "wisdom" refers to a wisdom identical to the wisdom of the multitudes, and "person" refers to a person identical to the persons of the multitudes; because one observes in this manner, there is no discrimination.
Furthermore, because his wisdom is the same as that of the multitude of beings, it is said that he is "equal to all wisdoms.
Moreover, since there is no Great Sage Buddha who is distinct from those sentient beings, it is said that he is "the same as sentient beings."
When one views persons and dharmas as equal, conceptual thoughts cease; therefore, there is no discrimination regarding all dharmas.

Regarding the passage "All is without loss, without turbidity, and without affliction": because the three karmas are free from transgression, all is without loss; because there is no loss, there is no turbidity; and because there is no turbidity, there is no affliction.

Regarding the passage "without action, without arising, without birth, and without cessation": the Dharma-body is unconditioned and transcends all contrived activity; who then could act upon it to cause it to arise, or bring it to birth and then cause it to cease?
“Fearless and without sorrow, without joy and without weariness, without attachment.
If there were arising and ceasing, these would be things to be feared; thus one would rejoice in arising and grieve over cessation.
Since joy and sorrow have already arisen, they are objects of aversion and attachment; yet the Dharma-body is neither of these.
It has not existed in the past, will not exist in the future, and does not exist in the present; it cannot be displayed through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The body of the Tathāgata is such as this; one should contemplate it in this way.
To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation.
"If one views it otherwise, it is called false viewing.
This concludes the summary of the Buddha’s body and exhorts one to observe it.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti:
"From where did you pass away to come and be born here? Below this, the second section clarifies the inconceivability of the manifested trace (*traces*).
This is divided into two parts:
first, explaining the meaning of birth as non-birth regarding Vimalakīrti; second, manifesting the immovable Buddha-land.

There are three reasons why Śāriputra poses this question: first, seeing that his spiritual virtue is marvelous and extraordinary, he infers that the place from which he comes must be sublime, and thus he asks about his origin; second, as it was stated above that one should contemplate the true mark of the self and that the true mark is non-arising, yet now there is manifest arising, [Śāriputra] asks about death and birth in order to fulfill the meaning of contemplating the self; third, [he asks] because he wishes to resolve the doubts of the assembly. Therefore, he asks: "From where have you come? and so forth. As for the phrase "from where have you come," this refers to the place of birth. As for the phrase "where are you going," this refers to the place of death. The meaning of these two questions is that if one can understand the principle of the non-arising of all phenomena, then one will not be deluded regarding the places of birth and death. Third, having already manifested the Dharma-body above, [the Buddha] now proceeds to reveal its functional traces;
therefore, he asks: "Vimalakīrti said:
'In the Dharma you have attained, is there any passing away or birth?'"
Śāriputra said:
"There is neither death nor birth.
If all dharmas lack the characteristics of death and birth, why do you ask, 'From where did you die to come and be born here?'"
"What do you think?
For example, if a magician were to conjure up men and women through illusion, would there truly be any death or birth among them?
Śāriputra replied:
"There is neither death nor birth.
Have you not heard the Buddha teach that all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion?
He replied:
It is so. If all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion, why do you ask: "From where did you pass away to come and be born here? Śāriputra!
"Cessation" refers to the characteristic of the deceptive dharma’s disintegration; "arising" refers to the characteristic of the deceptive dharma’s continuity.
Although the Bodhisattva ceases, he does not exhaust his roots of goodness;
although he arises, he does not increase various evils. Furthermore, both good and evil are merely deceptive dharmas of continuity and disintegration.
However, when ordinary beings are born, they increase in evil, and when they die, they are entirely good;
when Bodhisattvas are born, they increase in goodness, and when they die, they are entirely evil.
Although birth and death are the same for both, their increase and exhaustion are not identical. Yet, since both are but signs of falsehood and decay, how do they differ from illusions?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"There is a land named Abhirati, where the Buddha is titled Akṣobhya; it was from that land that this Vimalakīrti passed away to be born here."
Śāriputra said:
"It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!"
"This person is indeed able to renounce a pure land and come to delight in this place of much anger and harm.
Vimalakīrti said: "Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
When the sun rises, does it coincide with darkness?
He replied:
"No. When the sun rises, there is no darkness.
Vimalakīrti said:
For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?
The answer is:
it desires to illuminate and thereby dispel the darkness.
Vimalakīrti said:

"In this way, although a bodhisattva is born in impure buddha-fields for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they do not conjoin with ignorance and darkness; rather, they merely extinguish the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings. The preceding section distinguished non-arising; this section discusses the place of birth, manifesting in response to conditions to proclaim the Dharma, so that those who come to it may find benefit from the very beginning.
Non-arising is the Dharma-body; arising refers to the manifested traces.
Furthermore, when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they always rely upon the two truths: non-arising pertains to the ultimate truth, while arising pertains to the conventional truth.
"At that time, the great assembly was filled with longing, desiring to behold the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the world-system Abhirati.
Knowing the thoughts of the entire gathering, the Buddha addressed Vimalakīrti, saying:
'Good son!'"

The passage beginning with "For this assembly, he manifests the Land of Wonderful Joy, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, so that all may behold them" constitutes the second section, clarifying the reason for manifesting the land of Akṣobhya. There are three causes and conditions:
first, to cause those in this assembly to cultivate the practices for the Pure Land so that they may attain rebirth there;
second, to reveal the inconceivable virtues of Vimalakīrti.
Third, regarding his intention to return to the land of his original birth in Abhirati:
by relinquishing this pure land and entering this defiled realm, he manifests the conditions of the Great Being’s great compassion.
The text consists of four sections:

first, the great assembly’s desire to see [the Pure Land]; second, Vimalakīrti’s manifestation of that land; third, the benefits gained by the assembly at that time; and fourth, the return to their original location.
This is the first section.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

"Without rising from my seat, I shall bring forth the world-system of Abhirati—its Iron Ring Mountains, mountains, rivers, valleys, streams, great oceans, springs, and Mount Sumerus; its suns, moons, stars, and constellations; the palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and Brahmās; as well as the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; the cities, towns, and villages; the men and women, both young and old; and even the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, his Bodhi tree, and the various exquisite lotuses that perform the work of a Buddha throughout the ten directions."

There were three jeweled stairways leading from Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; by means of these jeweled stairways, the various devas would descend to pay their respects to the Tathāgata Acala and listen to and receive the Dharma teachings.
People of Jambudvīpa may also ascend its steps and rise up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to behold those devas.
The world-system Abhirati has thus accomplished such immeasurable merit that, from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven above down to the water’s edge below, it can be severed and taken up with his right hand.
"Like a potter’s wheel," and so forth: the second section clarifies the manifestation of the land.

"Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi and manifested supernatural powers, seizing the world of Abhirati with his right palm. Below this, the second section correctly clarifies the manifestation of the land, which consists of four parts:

Then the Bodhisattvas who have attained supernatural powers, the assembly of Śrāvakas, and the other devas and humans all raised their voices together, saying:"

"If there be anyone who obtains this sutra, they have already obtained the treasury of the Dharma-treasure.

"If there are those who read and recite it, explain its meaning, and practice according to the teaching, they shall be protected and remembered by all Buddhas. 13. Chapter on Dharma-Service (6). The thirteenth chapter, "On Dharma-Service," consists of three parts. The introduction and the main body have already been explained; next, the dissemination [of the teaching] shall be elucidated.
The dissemination [of the teaching] has two aspects:

Regarding the "Chapter on Dharma-Worship" (*Dharmapūjā-parivarta*): "Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna, the ultimate and definitive teaching.
To act according to what one has taught is to nourish one's own Dharma-body;
to teach according to what one has practiced is to nourish the Dharma-bodies of others.
Both of these accord with the Buddha’s mind and are thus offerings to the Buddha, termed "Dharma-offerings."
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the Deva-king’s praise of the Dharma and the person; second, the Tathāgata’s seal of approval and narration.
The first part consists of three sentences:
First, praising the Dharma heard; second, extolling the person capable of hearing it; third, making a vow to propagate and protect it.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha in the midst of the great assembly, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"Although I have heard hundreds of thousands of sutras from the Buddha and Mañjuśrī, I have never before heard this Sūtra of the Inconceivable Sovereign Supernatural Powers and the Definitive True Reality. This first sentence praises the Dharma.

Because works such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Dapin*) are extensive, they are difficult to consult; this [text], by contrast, is concise, and thus it is praised as something unprecedented. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"This person shall close off all evil destinies and open the gates to all virtues; they will be constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas;

they shall subdue those of external paths and destroy the enmity of Māra; they shall cultivate and purify Bodhi and dwell securely at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), treading the path traversed by the Tathāgatas. From here below, this is the second time the person is praised.
“World-Honored One!

If there are practitioners who uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the teaching, I shall provide offerings and respectful service together with my retinue. In whatever villages, towns, cities, mountain forests, or wildernesses this sutra may be found, I too, along with my retinue, will go to those places for the sake of hearing and receiving the Dharma. For those who have not yet developed faith, I shall cause them to give rise to it;
for those who already have faith, I shall act as their protectors.”
This was the third vow to extensively protect [the Dharma].
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Lord of Devas!

This sutra extensively explains the inconceivable *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
This second section clarifies the Buddha’s endorsement.

This first part is the initial description and praise of the Dharma.
"O Lord of Devas!

The first part correctly describes the praise; the second requires comparative evaluation.
This is the initial passage:
"O Lord of Devas!..."

Suppose that the trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, as densely packed as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, or forest thickets. "What do you think, Śakra, Lord of the Devas?
Is the merit planted by that person not indeed great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"It is much, World-Honored One!
That merit could not be fully exhausted even if explained for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

You should know that if these sons and daughters of good family hear this *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Liberation*, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice it, their merit will be far greater than that.
Why is this? Because the bodhi of all Buddhas is born from this.
The characteristics of the Good Awakening (Sudati) are immeasurable; for this reason, its merit is also immeasurable.”
This second point must be distinguished by its characteristics and measure.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"In the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Bhaiṣajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

The world was named Great Adornment, and the eon was named Adornment. The Buddha’s lifespan was twenty minor eons; his assembly of śrāvakas numbered sixty-six billion nayutas, and his assembly of bodhisattvas numbered one billion two hundred million.
"O Lord of Devas!

At that time, Ratnacchattra and his retinue made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, providing all necessities for his comfort for a full five kalpas.
After the five kalpas had passed, he addressed his thousand sons:
"You also should follow my example and all make offerings to the Buddha with a profound mind."

"Then the thousand sons, having received the command of their father the King, made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja for another full five kalpas, providing all that was needed for his peace and comfort.
Below this, the third section cites a past event to describe and confirm the Heavenly Emperor’s vow to provide extensive protection.
The text is divided into five sections:

This is the first passage:
"The king’s eldest son, named Candracchattra, sat alone in contemplation, thinking:
