What is meant by the 'offering of the Dharma'?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!
As for 'Dharma-offering,' it refers to the profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas. Below this, the second section correctly elucidates the Dharma-offering.
"Profound sutras" refers to those Mahāyāna sutras of definitive meaning that reach the ultimate conclusion.

Regarding the passage, "Difficult for all the world to believe and difficult to accept; subtle and difficult to see; pure and unstained; not something that can be attained merely through conceptual discrimination and reflection": the phrase "not merely through conceptual discrimination" means that it cannot be attained by the discrimination of ordinary wisdom.
That which is attained through contemplation must be obtained by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
furthermore, it can only be attained through right observation (*samyag-darśana*), and is not something attained through the contemplation that grasps at conceptualized marks.
“Compendium of the Bodhisattva Dharma-treasury.
Regarding the great illumination of the Buddha-dharma, there are generally two treasuries:
that which is taught for those of the Small Vehicle is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; [the other is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka].
It is taught for those of the Mahāyāna and is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Regarding the phrase "sealed by the seal of dhāraṇī," below this, *dhāraṇī* is practice, which takes mindfulness and wisdom as its essence.
To record the Dharma without forgetting it is mindfulness; to know that arising phenomena are non-arising is wisdom.
First is hearing and retaining, which means holding the teachings without forgetting them;
second is contemplation and reflection, which means grasping the meanings without losing them.
Because it upholds the meaning without loss, it cannot be altered; thus, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*).

Furthermore, there are many ways to explain "upholding"; this is the *dhāraṇī* of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because this sūtra is sealed by means of the true reality, it is called a "profound sūtra."
"Reaching the stage of non-retrogression":
by practicing this profound sutra, one will certainly attain non-retrogression.

"Accomplishing the six perfections, skillfully discerning their meanings, conforming to the Dharma of Bodhi, the foremost among all sutras, and entering great compassion"—because of compassion, one is able to know the profound sutras; because one knows the profound sutras, one necessarily enters into compassion. Since this sutra teaches Bodhisattvas to transform and benefit sentient beings, one may thus enter into great compassion.

"Free from all demonic activities and various false views, one accords with the law of dependent origination. Below this, it is stated that the causes and conditions taught in the profound sutras are neither definitively existent nor non-existent; therefore, one accords with dependent origination.

"Selflessness, personlessness, beinglessness, and lifelessness; emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-arising—these can cause sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). To first sit at the site of enlightenment is precisely to enter the Vajra Samādhi.
If discussed generally, all myriad practices are capable of giving rise to the Way and are thus called *bodhimaṇḍas*.
This profound sutra enables one to sit within these two *bodhimaṇḍas*.

"And it turns the wheel of Dharma, which is praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others; it enables sentient beings to enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, gathers the wisdom of all worthies and sages, and expounds the path practiced by all bodhisattvas. Relying on the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, it clearly proclaims the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation. Below this, those who explain impermanence without relying on the true mark destroy permanence and instead become attached to impermanence.

If one speaks of impermanence based on the true nature (*dharmatā*), then one subverts the notion of permanence without clinging to impermanence; this is what is meant by "clearly proclaiming the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "Able to save all sentient beings who violate the prohibitions," those who commit the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes cannot be saved by the Hīnayāna, whereas for the Mahāyāna, there is nothing that it does not rescue.

Regarding the passage, "The various Māras, non-Buddhists, and those who are greedily attached will cause [one] to feel fear": here, the non-Buddhists represent views (*dṛṣṭi*), and greedy attachment represents craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Profound sūtras can transform such craving and views; consequently, one feels fear toward that very craving and views.

"Commended by all Buddhas and noble sages; turning one's back on the suffering of birth and death and revealing the bliss of nirvana; as taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time"—from this point downward, the preceding section has correctly elucidated the Dharma.

"If one hears such sutras as these, and believes, understands, accepts, maintains, reads, and recites them"—this clarifies practicing in accordance with the Dharma, which accords with the Buddha's mind; this is what is meant by "making offerings."

"By the power of skillful means, one analyzes, explains, and clearly reveals [the Dharma] for the sake of all sentient beings; because of guarding the Dharma, this is called 'the offering of offerings. Below, this clarifies that one speaks according to practice, causing all people to deeply understand the Way and the Dharma.
Furthermore, when one nourishes the *dharmakāya* as described above, it is said to be in accord with the Buddha’s mind; this is called "Dharma-offering.

Moreover, the passage beginning with "furthermore, practicing according to the teaching regarding all phenomena, conforming to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), abandoning all false views, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), being certain that there is no self and no sentient beings, having no contradiction or dispute regarding causes, conditions, and karmic retribution, and being free from the notion of 'mine' (*mamakāra*)"—this section reiterates that practicing according to the teaching constitutes an offering.
"Rely on the meaning, not on the words.
Words constitute the teaching, while meaning constitutes the fundamental principle.
Since the teaching is used to clarify the principle—just as pointing with a finger indicates the moon—one must rely on the principle and not rely on the teaching.
“Rely on wisdom (jñāna), do not rely on consciousness (vijñāna).
Consciousness takes attachment as its nature, while wisdom takes the realization of principle as its function; therefore, one relies on wisdom and not on consciousness.
"Rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha), do not rely on sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
Since the meanings known by wisdom are of both definitive and provisional types, one must rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not on those of provisional meaning.
"Rely on the Dharma, not on the person. Although the Dharma is propagated by persons, it is not necessarily the case that all persons can fully conform to the Dharma.
The Dharma possesses fixed standards, whereas persons lack constant principles; therefore, rely on the Dharma and not on the person.
There is another sequence of the Dharma: first, rely on the Dharma and not on the person, as explained above;

second, rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on those of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Although one has previously discarded the person to take up the Dharma, since the Dharma itself possesses both definitive and provisional aspects, this next step distinguishes against the provisional in order to cause one to grasp the definitive.
Third, rely on the meaning and not on the words: since definitive sūtras contain both principle and teaching, one must rely on the principle and not on the teaching.

Fourth, rely on wisdom and not on consciousness: the principle known by consciousness is insufficient to rely upon; only the principle known by wisdom can be relied upon; therefore, one must rely on wisdom and not on consciousness.
“In accordance with the characteristics of phenomena, there is nothing entered and nothing returned to.

Because ignorance is ultimately extinguished, volitional formations are also ultimately extinguished; continuing in this way until because birth is ultimately extinguished, old age and death are also ultimately extinguished.”
"By contemplating in this way, one sees that the twelve links of dependent origination possess no characteristic of exhaustion.
Question:
Cessation is itself exhaustion; since you now say there is no exhaustion, how can it have been said above that they are "ultimately extinguished"?
Answer:
Previously, in contrast to the false notion that there is arising, it was said that there is ultimate cessation.
However, since the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning, they now have no cessation; because there is no cessation, one speaks of inexhaustibility.
The previous statement, "ultimate cessation," refuted the ordinary person's notion of arising;
the present term, "inexhaustible," rejects the two vehicles' notion of cessation.
Therefore, the subsequent phrase says, "no further views arise."

"Those who no longer give rise to views" refers to having transcended the views of birth held by ordinary beings above, and now not giving rise to the views of cessation held by the followers of the Two Vehicles.
"No longer giving rise to views is called the supreme offering of the Dharma."
The performance of the Dharma-offering is the most supreme.
There are two ways to distinguish the Dharma-offering:
if one gives rise to views regarding the Dharma, it is not the most supreme Dharma-offering.
"If one does not give rise to views regarding the Dharma, this is called the supreme Dharma-offering.
The Buddha told Śakra:
"The prince Candracchattra, having heard such a teaching from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja, attained the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti)."
Third, one obtains benefit through the offering of hearing the Dharma.

With a supple mind and compliant wisdom, one is capable of receiving the true reality (*dharmatā*), yet has not yet reached the stage of non-arising; this is called the stage of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience in accordance with truth).
There are two types of compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*):
first, that which exists in the thirty mental states prior to the stages; second, that which exists from the sixth stage downward.
Non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) likewise has two types:
One was in the first stage (*bhūmi*), and the other resided in the seventh stage.
They immediately took off their precious robes and ornaments to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I shall perform the offering of the Dharma and protect the True Dharma; I pray that you will compassionately establish me through your majestic spiritual power, so that I may subdue the enmity of Māra and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in his deep mind, prophesied to him, saying:

At that time, Prince Candracchattra, having seen the purity of the Dharma and heard the Buddha’s prophecy, left the household life out of faith. "Because the bhikṣu Candracchattra protected and upheld the Dharma and practiced with diligent vigor, he transformed one hundred trillion people within this very body and established them in non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; fourteen *nayutas* of people deeply resolved their minds toward the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and immeasurable sentient beings attained rebirth in the heavens."

Previously, it was explained that he attained the *kṣānti* of compliance; now it is said that he has acquired the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), which refers to the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
Because he has fully attained these two types of *kṣānti*, he practices exactly as taught, which is called the "Dharma-offering";
furthermore, because he can teach according to his practice, enabling many people to realize the Way, this is also called the Dharma-offering.
"O Lord of Devas!

The king’s thousand sons are none other than the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
beginning with Kālakarṇin, they culminate in the Tathāgata named Ruci.

This concludes the fourth assembly, which correlates the past and the present.

Regarding the "Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa): when the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven observed the beginning of this kalpa, they saw a thousand precious lotus flowers emerge from within the waters; knowing thereby that one thousand Buddhas would appear in the world, they named this kalpa the "Auspicious Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa).
“Worthy” (xian) means “good” (shan).

first, prior to the praise; now, for the second time, the entrustment is clarified.

This chapter is divided into five sections:

first, the entrustment to Maitreya;
second, Maitreya’s acceptance.
The three Buddhas praised him, saying:

'Maitreya!'"

"I now entrust to you this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas. As for why he did not entrust it to Ānanda, it was because he lacked the supernormal powers (ṛddhibala) necessary to propagate and proclaim it widely.

Question:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the first esoteric teaching, it was entrusted to the bodhisattvas;
because the *Prajñāpāramitā* is not an esoteric teaching, it was entrusted to the śrāvakas."
If this sutra does not clarify that śrāvakas receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, then it is not a secret teaching; why, then, is it entrusted to bodhisattvas?
Answer:
There are two kinds of *pāpa* (evil/obstruction): [text continues].
The first is common to the three vehicles;
the second is taught exclusively for bodhisattvas.
Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*) is the Prajñāpāramitā common to the three vehicles, it was therefore entrusted to the śrāvakas.

Although this sutra is not esoteric, it uniquely elucidates the inconceivable dharma-gate of the bodhisattvas; as it is beyond the knowledge of those in lower stages, how could it be fathomed by the followers of the two vehicles?
Therefore, I entrust this to the Bodhisattvas and do not rely upon the Śrāvakas.

"Such sūtras as these, during the final age after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, you must use your supernormal powers to widely proclaim and disseminate them throughout Jambudvīpa, ensuring they are never cut off."

Why is this? In future ages there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others, who will resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and take delight in the Great Dharma.
"If they do not hear such sutras as these, they will lose this excellent benefit.

People of this kind, upon hearing such sutras, will surely have much faith and joy, give rise to a sense of rare wonder, and receive them upon their shoulders; one should preach them extensively according to the benefits that each sentient being ought to obtain. Herein, the preceding clause is the formal entrustment to Maitreya, while this section is the exhortation for Maitreya to proclaim [the teaching].
“Maitreya, you should know that there are two characteristics of a bodhisattva. What are these two?
First, they delight in miscellaneous phrases and ornate literary embellishments;
second, they do not fear profound meanings and are able to enter them as they truly are.
If one delights in miscellaneous phrases and ornate literary embellishments, it should be known that this is a bodhisattva who is newly trained.

"If one has no fear regarding such profound sūtras that are undefiled and unattached, is able to enter into them, and having heard them, purifies the mind, upholds, recites, and practices according to the teaching, it should be known that this person has long cultivated the path of practice. Below this, the first two lines clarify the entrustment for wide dissemination; now, the current section clarifies the ritual for transmitting the Dharma as an admonition and encouragement.
There are three pairs in total:

first, a pair that generally clarifies the two types of persons—those who are shallow and those who are deep; second, a pair that must distinguish the two faults of the person receiving the Dharma; and third, a pair that clearly explains the two errors of the person preaching the Dharma.
First, regarding the clarification of the two types of individuals—those of shallow and deep capacity: if one delights in manifold phrases, one should bestow upon them the literary text;
if one delights in the profound Dharma, one should instruct them in its meaning.

The literary expression is the "trap and snare" for the subtle meaning; yet those of new learning have shallow wisdom and are unable to forget the words to grasp the principle, adhering instead only to the embellishments of the text.
As for those who cherish the meaning, the subtle meaning is exceedingly profound—words are forgotten and thought ceases; were it not for one of intellectual courage, who could possibly receive it?
Therefore, based on the meaning of the text, I have distinguished the depth and shallowness of these two types of persons. "Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which those who are newly trained are unable to reach a definitive certainty regarding the profound Dharma."
What are these two?
First, upon hearing profound sutras never heard before, they are struck with alarm and fear, giving rise to doubt; unable to accord with them, they slander and do not believe them, saying:
"I have never heard this before; from where has it come?"

Second, if there are those who protect, uphold, and explain such profound sutras, one is unwilling to draw near to them, make offerings to them, or honor them; or at times, one even casts blame and faults upon them.

"Having these two dharmas, one should know that this newly initiated bodhisattva brings about self-destruction and injury, and is unable to discipline his mind within the profound Dharma. Below this, the second pair clarifies the two faults of those who receive the Dharma.
First one destroys the Dharma, and next one slanders others; therefore, this serves as a warning.
At first, hearing it causes alarm; upon investigation, doubt arises; and in the end, slander is provoked once more—this is indeed the fault of destroying the Dharma.
One who slanders others is unable to consult with, respect, or support them, but instead speaks of their faults. "Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva, though they have faith and understanding in the profound dharma, still brings about self-destruction and cannot attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
What are these two?
First, to treat newly initiated bodhisattvas with contempt and fail to instruct them;
second, although one has faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination.
"Regarding 'these are the two dharmas' and below, this third pair explains the two faults of those who preach the Dharma:

first, the external fault; although they possess profound understanding, they have not yet put it into practice, and being self-exalting and arrogant toward others, they are unable to instruct or guide listeners.
Second, the internal fault; although they have attained the profound Dharma, they form the notion that there is something to be gained, and thus grasp at signs and engage in discrimination."
When Maitreya Bodhisattva had heard this being spoken, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented!”
"As the Buddha has taught, I shall distance myself from such evils and uphold the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

If, in future ages, there are good men and virtuous people who seek the Mahāyāna, you should cause them to obtain such sūtras as these in their hands; grant them the power of mindfulness so that they may receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain them to others.
“World-Honored One!

If, in the future final age, there should be those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others, you should know that this is established through the supernatural power of Maitreya. Below this is the second instance of Maitreya receiving his mandate.
As for the power of mindfulness, it causes what has been heard not to be forgotten.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Maitreya!
It is as you have said.
The Buddha rejoices with you. This concludes the third section: the Tathāgata’s expression of praise.
"Then all these bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:

'After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we too shall widely proclaim and disseminate this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout the lands of the ten directions; furthermore, we shall guide and instruct those who preach the Dharma, enabling them to obtain this sutra. Below this is the second section, in which the various bodhisattvas vow to propagate the teaching themselves.
Maitreya shall disseminate it in this land, and the various bodhisattvas shall propagate it throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"Wherever there may be cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses, and wherever this sutra is read, recited, or explained, I shall lead my retinue of officials to that place for the sake of hearing the Dharma. I will protect those individuals within a radius of one hundred *yojanas*, ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them can find such an opening. Thus ends the third and fourth kings' vow to provide protection.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
“Receive and uphold this sutra, and propagate it widely.
Ānanda said:
"Yes, indeed!
World-Honored One, I have already accepted and observed the essential precepts."
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is named the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, and it is also named the 'Inconceivable Dharma-gate of Liberation. You should uphold it thus. Below this is the fourth section, in which the Buddha commands his attendant to uphold the teaching.
First, the command; second, receiving the decree with the head bowed; third, inquiring after names; fourth, answering the title.

Following the passage, "When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the rest, as well as all the great assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy," we come to the fifth section: the assembly rejoices, believes, accepts, and practices accordingly.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Six.
